116.5.oldText: I got up late. On waking I lay in bed a long time, giving in to laziness. O God, help and strengthen me that I may walk in Your ways! Read the Scriptures, but without proper feeling. At the time I gave him no answer. Now I replayed every detail of that meeting and in my mind gave him the most vicious and bitter replies. I caught myself and drove away that thought only when I realized I was burning with anger — but I did not repent enough. Afterward Boris Drubetskoy came and began telling various stories. His visit irritated me from the start, and I said something unpleasant to him. He responded. I lost my temper and said much that was rude and even cruel to him. He fell silent, and I only came to my senses when it was too late. My God, I simply cannot get along with him. The reason is my own selfishness. I put myself above him and so become much worse than he is, for he is patient with my rudeness while I harbor contempt for him. O God, grant that in his presence I may instead see my own failings, and behave so that he too may benefit. 226.2.oldText: With each fresh blow, the chances of survival for those still standing grew slimmer. The regiment stood in battalion columns three hundred paces apart, but all the men shared the same mood — taciturn and somber. Talk was rare in the ranks and ceased altogether each time the thud of a successful hit was heard with the cry "Stretchers!" Most of the time, on their officers' orders, the men sat on the ground. One, having removed his cap, carefully adjusted and tightened its lining; another rubbed dry clay between his palms to polish his bayonet; another fingered his belt strap and tugged at its buckle; another smoothed and refolded his leg wrappings and put his boots back on. Some built little houses from clods of plowed earth, or braided baskets from the straw in the field. All seemed entirely absorbed in these tasks. When men were killed or wounded, when rows of stretchers passed, or when great masses of the enemy came into view through the smoke, no one paid any attention. But when their own artillery or cavalry advanced, or their own infantry was seen moving forward, approving shouts were heard on all sides. Yet the liveliest interest was drawn to events completely unrelated to the battle — as if the minds of these morally exhausted men found relief in everyday, ordinary things. An artillery battery was passing in front of the regiment. A horse from an ammunition cart got its leg caught over a trace. "Hey, look at that trace horse! Get her leg out! She'll fall! They can't see it!" — the same cries rang out from every part of the regiment. Another time, a small brown dog of unknown origin trotted purposefully in front of the ranks with its tail stiffly upright, until suddenly a shell landed nearby, and it yelped, tucked its tail between its legs, and bolted sideways. Howls and shrieks of laughter erupted across the whole regiment. But such distractions lasted only a moment, and for eight hours the men had been idle, without food, in constant fear of death, and their pale, gloomy faces grew ever paler and gloomier.

336.1.oldText: He did not repeat to himself with a sickening feeling of shame the words he had spoken, or think: "Oh, why didn't I say that?" and "Whatever made me say 'I love you'?" On the contrary, he now replayed in his mind every word he or Natasha had said, down to the smallest detail of her face and smile, and wanted to add nothing and take nothing away. He only wished he could say it all again. "Was it right when she said, 'Leave it to me'? Did she really see into my soul? Yes, she did," Pierre told himself. "And she's wonderful! 'Something fine!'—how she said it! And her eyes. And how she blushed when she said: 'I'll very much look forward to your return'... She loves me. Yes, she loves me." That was the only worry that often troubled Pierre. He made no plans now. The happiness before him seemed so inconceivable that if only he could reach it, there would be nothing beyond. Everything ended there.

336.4.oldText: When people suggested he enter the civil service, or when the war or general political affairs were discussed on the assumption that everyone's well-being depended on some particular turn of events, he would listen with his mild, compassionate smile, and startle everyone with his strange comments. But those who thought they understood Pierre, as well as those who didn't, all felt at this time that he was a delightful and extraordinary person—generous, gentle, clever, cheerful, and magnanimous.

338.12.oldText: It lies in the fact that a historical figure like Alexander I, standing at the highest possible pinnacle of human power, in the blinding light of history focused upon him—exposed to the strongest influences imaginable: the intrigues, flattery, and self-deception inseparable from power, and feeling a responsibility for everything happening in Europe at every moment of his life—proved to be, not fifty years ago but today, not a person of particularly virtuous character. That is what the historians' criticisms amount to.

338.13.oldText: But even if we assume that Alexander was mistaken fifty years ago in his idea of what was good for the people, we must also assume that the historian who judges him will, after some time, also turn out to be wrong in his understanding of what is good for humanity. This assumption is all the more natural and inevitable because the development of history shows us that every year, with every new writer, what we consider good for humanity changes. What once seemed good—giving Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance—is later regarded as harmful. What seems harmful—the Napoleonic wars, the spread of revolutionary ideas—is later recognized as good.

339.9.oldText: We need only acknowledge that we do not know the purpose of the European upheavals, and that we only know the facts—that is, the killings, first in France, then in Italy, Africa, Prussia, Austria, Spain, and Russia—and that the movements from west to east and from east to west form the essential substance of those events. Only then will we no longer need to see something exceptional—some stroke of genius—in the characters of Napoleon and Alexander, and will no longer need to attribute the event to some individual's specific quality.

340.0.oldText: The fundamental significance of the European events at the start of the nineteenth century lies in the mass movement of European peoples from west to east and then from east to west. The initial impulse for the westward movement came from France. For the French to unite into a military force capable of invading the East, they first needed to combine into a sufficiently large group, renounce their established customs and traditions, and—through the process of war and campaigning—develop a leader who could stand at the head of the coming military movement.

340.3.oldText: His colleagues' incompetence, his opponents' weakness and insignificance, the brazenness of his lies, and his dazzling, self-confident narrow-mindedness raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant quality of the soldiers in the Italian campaign, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his own childish boldness and self-assurance win him military glory. Countless so-called coincidences accompany him everywhere. The disfavor into which he falls with the rulers of France works in his favor. His attempts to change his career path fail: he isn't accepted into the Russian army, and his appointment to Turkey comes to nothing.

340.10.oldText: Chance—millions of chances—give him power, and all people, as if by common agreement, work to confirm that power. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him; chance shapes the character of Russia's Paul I, who recognizes his authority; chance produces a plot against him that not only fails to harm him but strengthens his power. Chance throws the Duke of Enghien into his hands and accidentally compels him to kill him, thereby convincing the crowd more effectively than any other means that he has the right to rule, since he possesses the power and the will to use it. Chance arranges it so that though he strains every nerve to prepare an expedition against England—which would certainly have destroyed him—he never carries out that plan, and instead falls upon Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a battle. Chance and genius give him victory after victory. Everything serves him. He is invincible.

340.11.oldText: Like probing movements before a battle, the western forces push eastward several times—in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809—gathering strength and growing. In 1811, the group of people formed in France fuses into one enormous mass with the peoples of central Europe. As this group grows, the man who stands at its head gains more and more justification for his power. During those ten years of preparation, this man forms connections with all the crowned heads of Europe. The rulers of the world, stripped naked by this man, try to oppose him with the ideals of reason and justice. But these seem weak and ridiculous before his ideal of glory and greatness, which makes no sense yet still exerts its force. In their efforts to show him that his plans are wrong, these rulers eagerly humiliate themselves before him. The King of Prussia sends his wife to seek the great man's mercy; the Emperor of Austria considers it a favor that this man accepts the daughter of the Kaisers into his bed. The Pope, guardian of all that the nations hold sacred, uses religion to promote the great man's power. It is not so much Napoleon who prepares himself for the fulfillment of his role as everyone around him who prepares him for the immense responsibility he is about to bear. There is no act, no crime or petty deception, that he commits which is not immediately reflected in the mouths of those around him as a great deed.

344.3.oldText: Having started farming out of necessity, Nicholas soon grew so devoted to it that it became his favorite—and nearly his only—occupation. He was a plain, practical farmer. He didn't like innovations, especially the English methods that were then coming into vogue. He laughed at theoretical treatises on agriculture, had no interest in factories or expensive crops, and didn't obsess over any one part of his operation to the exclusion of the rest. What he always kept in mind was the estate as a whole, not any particular component. What mattered to him was not nitrogen in the soil or oxygen in the air, not special plows or fertilizers, but the principal instrument through which nitrogen, oxygen, plows, and fertilizers all worked—that is, the laboring peasant. When Nicholas first took up farming and began to understand its various branches, it was the peasant who especially engaged his attention. He saw the peasant not merely as a tool but as an end in himself and as a judge. At first he studied the peasant closely, trying to understand what he needed and what he considered good and bad, and only pretended to give orders while in fact learning from the peasants, their methods, and their language. Only when he understood the peasants' tastes and aspirations, had learned to speak their language and grasp the hidden meaning behind their words, and felt himself one of them, did he begin to manage them boldly—that is, to fulfill toward them the duty expected of him.

344.10.oldText: Countess Mary was jealous of this passion of her husband's and regretted that she couldn't share it. She couldn't understand why he was so particularly excited and happy when, having gotten up at dawn and spent the whole morning in the fields or on the threshing floor, he came back to tea from the sowing, mowing, or harvesting. She couldn't understand what made him so delighted when he talked enthusiastically about the prosperous, hardworking peasant Matvei Ermilov who had been up all night with his family carting sheaves, or about having gotten all his grain in before anyone else.

345.8.oldText: Nicholas said nothing. He turned crimson, left her side, and paced up and down the room. He understood what she was crying about, but couldn't immediately agree in his heart that what he had done since childhood—what he considered perfectly normal—was wrong.

347.19.oldText: It happened quite often that in a moment of irritation, husband and wife would argue; but long afterward Pierre would discover—to his surprise and delight—that in his wife's ideas and actions he found the very thought she had argued against, stripped of everything extraneous that his own masculine expression of it had introduced. And he found it there in its purest form.

349.4.oldText: Young Nicholas—now a slim boy of fifteen, delicate and intelligent, with curly light-brown hair and beautiful eyes—was delighted because Uncle Pierre, as he called him, was the object of his rapturous and passionate devotion. No one had deliberately tried to inspire this devotion in him; he had come to it on his own. In his imagination, Pierre was a hero. From half-remembered stories about Pierre and Natasha, from the emotion with which Pierre spoke of the boy's dead father, from the careful, reverent tenderness with which Natasha spoke of him, the boy—who was only just beginning to guess what love is—formed the idea that his father had loved Natasha and had, when dying, bequeathed her to his friend. And that father—whom the boy did not remember—seemed to him a divinity who could not be imagined in human form, and of whom he never thought without a swelling heart and tears of sorrow and enthusiasm. So the boy was happy that Pierre had come.

349.10.oldText: Though he was the most absent-minded and forgetful of men, Pierre had managed—with the help of a list his wife had drawn up—to buy everything, not forgetting his mother-in-law's and brother-in-law's commissions, nor the dress material as a gift for Belova, nor toys for his nephews. In the early days of his marriage, this demand that he remember everything had struck him as strange, and he'd been impressed by the serious way Natasha insisted that he not forget a single item she'd entrusted to him, and by how offended she was when he returned from his first trip having forgotten everything. But in time he grew accustomed to it. Knowing that Natasha never asked him to buy anything for herself, and only gave him commissions for others when he offered, he now took an unexpected, childlike pleasure in buying presents for the whole household—never forgetting anything. If he deserved a scolding from Natasha, it was only for buying too many things and things that were too expensive.

350.0.oldText: When Pierre and his wife entered the drawing room, the countess was in one of her usual states in which she needed the mental effort of playing patience. So—though out of habit she greeted him with the words she always used when Pierre or her son returned: "High time, my dear! We've been waiting and waiting. Thank heaven you're here!"—and when she received her presents said the same words she always said: "It's not the gift that counts, my dear... thank you for thinking of an old woman like me..."—it was clear that Pierre's arrival annoyed her at that moment because it distracted her from her unfinished game. She finished the game and only then examined the presents. They consisted of a card box of splendid workmanship, a bright-blue Sevres teacup with shepherdesses painted on it and a lid, and a gold snuffbox with the late count's portrait on it, which Pierre had commissioned from a miniaturist in Petersburg. The countess had been wanting this for a long time, but now she didn't feel like crying and so she looked at the portrait indifferently and focused instead on the card box.

350.1.oldText: "Thank you, my dear, you've cheered me up," she said, as she always did. "But best of all you've brought yourself back—this has been absolutely ridiculous. You really must scold your wife! What are we to do with her? Without you she's like a madwoman! She doesn't see anything, doesn't remember anything," she said with her usual phrases. "Look, Anna Timofeevna," she added to her companion, "see what a fine card box my son has brought me!"

350.2.oldText: Belova admired the presents and was delighted with her dress material.

350.3.oldText: Though Pierre, Natasha, Nicholas, Countess Mary, and Denisov had much to talk about that they couldn't discuss in front of the old countess—not that anything was hidden from her, but because she had fallen so far behind that if they had started talking about anything in front of her, they would have had to answer her irrelevant questions and repeat things she'd already been told. They would have had to explain that so-and-so was dead, or so-and-so was married, which she would forget again the next time—yet they sat at tea around the samovar in the drawing room, and Pierre answered the old countess's questions that were of no interest to anyone, telling her that Prince Vasili had aged, and that Countess Maria Alexeyevna sent her regards and remembered her kindly, and so on.

350.4.oldText: This kind of conversation, interesting to no one yet unavoidable, continued through teatime. All the grown-up members of the family were assembled around the round tea table where Sonya presided by the samovar. The children with their tutors and governesses had already had tea and could be heard in the next room. Everyone sat in their usual places at tea; Nicholas sat by the stove at a small table where his tea was passed to him; Milka, an old gray borzoi bitch, the daughter of the original Milka, with a face full of black spots, lay in an armchair beside him. Denisov, his curly hair now half-gray, his mustache and whiskers showing it too, sat next to Countess Mary with his general's unbuttoned tunic. Pierre sat between his wife and the old countess. He was telling them what he knew might interest the old lady and what she could understand. He talked about external social events and about those people who had once formed the circle of the old countess's contemporaries—who had once been a real, living, distinct group but who were now for the most part scattered over the world, finishing their earthly course like she was. But to the countess these contemporaries seemed to be the only serious and real society. Natasha could tell by Pierre's animation that his trip had been interesting and that he had much to say that he couldn't talk about in front of the old countess.

350.5.oldText: Denisov, not being a member of the family, didn't understand Pierre's caution and—being besides very interested in what was going on in Petersburg—kept urging Pierre to tell them about what had happened with the Semyonovsky regiment, or about Arakcheyev, or about the Bible Society. Pierre would occasionally get carried away and start talking, but Nicholas and Natasha always steered him back to the health of Prince Ivan Ivanovich and Countess Maria Antonovna.

350.6.oldText: "Well, and all this nonsense—Gossner and Tatarinova?" Denisov asked. "Is that really still going on?"

351.10.oldText: Nicholas, who didn't share Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was very serious and weighty business, and the fact that A had been appointed Minister of This and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such-and-such and the minister something else, all seemed very important to him. And he thought it was his duty to take an interest in it and to question Pierre accordingly.

352.25.oldText: "Well, I don't think you need to blame yourself on his account. Everything the most devoted mother could do for a son, you've done and are doing for him. And of course I'm glad of it. He's a fine boy, a fine boy! This evening he listened to Pierre in a kind of trance. And do you know—when we stood up to go to supper, I looked over and he'd smashed everything on my desk to bits, and he told me about it himself right away. I've never known him to lie. A fine boy, really!" Nicholas repeated, pleased with his assessment.

352.31.oldText: Countess Mary listened to her husband and understood everything he told her. She knew that when he thought aloud like this he would sometimes ask what he'd been saying, and be annoyed if he noticed she'd been thinking about something else. But she had to make a considerable effort to pay attention, because what he said didn't interest her at all. She looked at him and—rather than thinking—felt something else entirely. She felt a submissive, tender love for this man who would never understand everything she understood, and she seemed to love him all the more for that, with a touch of passionate tenderness. Besides this feeling, which absorbed her entirely, she was also thinking about her children: she wasn't thinking about them, exactly, but feeling their existence—the need to watch over their health, to feed, to educate. She mentally counted them over, made sure she hadn't forgotten any, and felt at peace.

353.3.oldText: Natasha told Pierre about her brother's life, about how she had suffered and felt dead inside during Pierre's absence, and how she was fonder than ever of Mary, and how Mary was better than her in every way. In saying this, Natasha was genuinely convinced that Mary was better, but she also expected Pierre to disagree with her—and he did.

354.9.oldText: In the first place, the historian describes the activity of individuals who in his opinion directed humanity. One historian considers only monarchs, generals, and ministers as such people, while another includes orators, scholars, reformers, philosophers, and poets as well. But all historians agree that these individuals expressed the will of their time, and that their activity was the direction in which the historical movement flowed.

355.1.oldText: Biographical historians and historians of individual nations understand this force as a power inherent in heroes and rulers. In their accounts, events happen solely through the will of a Napoleon, an Alexander, or whatever person they happen to be describing. The answers these historians give to the question of what force drives events are satisfying only as long as there is just one historian for each event. But as soon as historians of different nations and perspectives begin describing the same event, the answers they give immediately lose all meaning, because this force is understood by each historian not only differently but often in completely opposite ways.

355.3.oldText: According to this view, the power of historical figures—represented as the product of many forces—can no longer be treated as a force that itself produces events. Yet in most cases, universal historians still use the concept of power as a force that independently produces events, treating it as both cause and effect at the same time.

355.6.oldText: A specialist historian describing the campaign of 1813 or the restoration of the Bourbons plainly asserts that these events were produced by the will of Alexander. But the universal historian Gervinus, refuting this view, tries to prove that the campaign of 1813 and the restoration of the Bourbons were caused not only by Alexander but also by Stein, Metternich, Madame de Stael, Talleyrand, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others. The historian has evidently broken down Alexander's power into its components: Talleyrand, Chateaubriand, and the rest. But the sum of these components—that is, the interaction of Chateaubriand, Talleyrand, Madame de Stael, and the others—obviously does not equal the whole result. The fact that millions of Christian men killed one another and devastated Europe was clearly not caused only by these individuals' activity. And therefore, the universal historian—after having broken down Alexander's power into components and proved them insufficient—must again accept the unexplained force called "power" and recognize it as the influence of great men on events, which is precisely the same thing the specialist historian said.

355.9.oldText: The cultural historians are perfectly consistent with their predecessors, the universal historians. If historical events can be explained by the fact that certain people treated one another in certain ways, why not explain them by the fact that certain people wrote certain books? Out of the vast number of indicators that accompany every living phenomenon, these historians select the indicator of intellectual activity and declare it to be the cause. But despite all their efforts to prove that the cause of events lies in intellectual activity, only with great reluctance can one agree that there is any connection between intellectual activity and the movement of peoples—and it is quite impossible to admit that intellectual activity guides the actions of people, because phenomena like the brutal murders of the French Revolution, which resulted from preaching about human equality, do not support such a conclusion.

355.10.oldText: But even granting all the cleverly constructed arguments with which these histories are filled—granting that nations are governed by some undefined force called an "idea"—history's essential question still remains unanswered. To the former power of monarchs and the influence of advisors and other individuals, a new force has now been added: the power of ideas. But how this new force is connected to events—that is, how one particular idea out of the millions of ideas that exist gives rise to a particular event—still needs to be explained.

355.11.oldText: Undoubtedly some relationship exists between all people who live at the same time, and so it is possible to find connections between the intellectual activity of people and their historical movements, just as connections can be found between the movements of humanity and trade, handicrafts, gardening, or anything else you care to name.

357.16.oldText: Some historians—those biographical and specialist historians already mentioned—who in their simplicity fail to grasp the question of what power means, seem to assume that the collective will of the people is unconditionally transferred to historical figures, and therefore when describing any power they treat it as the one real, absolute, and inviolable power.

357.19.oldText: Each historian, according to his own idea of what constitutes a nation's progress, looks for the key conditions in the greatness, wealth, freedom, or enlightenment of the citizens of France or some other country. But not only do historians contradict each other about the nature of this program—even admitting that one such program exists for all nations—the facts of history almost always contradict the theory. If the conditions on which power is delegated are a nation's wealth, freedom, or enlightenment, why did a Louis XIV or an Ivan the Terrible live out their reigns in peace, while a Louis XVI or a Charles I were executed by their peoples? To this question the historians have no answer. If the connection between rulers and peoples is based on conditions, then why should people who violate those conditions be punished—punished by execution or by disgrace—by the very people who put them in power on those conditions?

357.28.oldText: Is the movement of the peoples during the Crusades explained by the lives and activity of the Godfreys and the Louises and their ladies? For us, that movement of peoples from west to east—without leaders, with a crowd of vagabonds and Peter the Hermit—remains incomprehensible. And still more incomprehensible is the cessation of that movement just when a rational and sacred goal for the Crusades—the liberation of Jerusalem—had been clearly set by the historic leaders. Popes, kings, and knights encouraged people to free the Holy Land; but the people did not go, because the unknown cause that had previously driven them to move no longer existed.

358.6.oldText: "If the animals at the front of the herd change, this happens because the collective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to another, depending on whether the animal is or isn't leading them in the direction chosen by the whole herd." This is the answer given by historians who assume the collective will of the masses is transferred to rulers on certain conditions which they regard as known.

358.14.oldText: On one hand, reflection shows that the expression of a person's will—his words—are only part of the total activity expressed in an event, such as a war or a revolution. And so, without invoking some incomprehensible, supernatural force—a miracle—one cannot accept that words can be the immediate cause of the movement of millions of people.

358.15.oldText: On the other hand, even if we admitted that words can be the cause of events, history shows that the expression of historical figures' wills in most cases produces no effect at all—that is, their orders are often not carried out, and sometimes the very opposite of what they commanded takes place.

358.16.oldText: Without admitting divine intervention in human affairs, we cannot regard "power" as the cause of events.

358.17.oldText: Power, from the standpoint of experience, is merely the relationship that exists between the expression of someone's will and the carrying out of that will by others.

358.18.oldText: To explain the conditions of that relationship, we must first establish a concept of the expression of will, referring it to man and not to God.

359.5.oldText: For an order to be reliably carried out, a person must command what can actually be done. But knowing what can and what cannot be done is impossible—not only in the case of Napoleon's invasion of Russia, where millions of people participated, but even in the simplest event—because in either case millions of obstacles may arise.

359.6.oldText: Our mistaken belief that an event is caused by the command that precedes it comes from the fact that, after the event has taken place, out of thousands of commands only those few that happened to match the event are remembered as having been carried out. We forget about the others because they didn't match the event and therefore weren't executed.

360.13.oldText: Examining only those expressions of will by historical persons which, as commands, were connected with events, historians have assumed that the events depended on those commands. But examining the events themselves and the connection in which the historical persons stood to the people, we have found that historical persons and their commands are dependent on events.

361.17.oldText: No matter how often experiment and reasoning show a man that under the same conditions, with the same character, he will do the same thing as before—yet when he approaches for the thousandth time an action that always ends the same way, he feels just as sure as ever that he can act however he wishes. Every man, savage or sage, however irrefutably reason and experience prove to him that it is impossible to imagine two different actions under precisely identical conditions, feels that without this absurd notion—which constitutes the essence of freedom—he cannot imagine life.

361.27.oldText: They say and write and print that the soul and freedom do not exist, that the life of man is expressed by muscular movements, and muscular movements are determined by nervous activity; that the soul and free will do not exist because at some unknown period of time we descended from apes. They say and write and print this not because they suspect that this is what the natural scientists' arguments actually lead to (for you can't cut off a thought in the middle), but because otherwise—if man has no freedom—it would be impossible to live. And man needs to live and to act.

362.10.oldText: A drowning man who grabs another and drags him under; a hungry mother exhausted from nursing who steals food; a soldier trained in discipline who kills a defenseless man on orders—these all seem less guilty, less free, and more subject to the law of necessity, to anyone who knows the circumstances of their actions. And conversely, a man who commits murder out of jealousy with no apparent provocation seems more free and less subject to the law of necessity. In every case, our idea of freedom and necessity depends on the circumstances under which the action took place.

362.25.oldText: When we do not at all understand the cause of an action—whether it is a crime, a good deed, or something morally neutral—we attribute the greatest amount of freedom to it. In the case of a crime, we most urgently demand punishment; in the case of a virtuous act, we rate its merit most highly; in the morally neutral case, we see the most individuality, originality, and independence. But if even one of the countless causes is known to us, we concede a certain amount of necessity and are less insistent in our demand for punishment, less appreciative of the virtue, and less ready to attribute freedom to the seemingly original action.

363.4.oldText: (2) However closely we bring the time of judgment to the time of the deed, we never get a notion of freedom in time. For if I examine an action committed a second ago, I must still recognize it as not free, because it is irrevocably linked to the moment at which it was committed. Can I raise my arm? I raise it; but I ask myself: could I have not raised it at the moment that has already passed? To convince myself that I could have, I don't raise my arm the next moment. But the moment I was asking about was not now—it is already irrecoverably past, and the arm I then raised was in the very air through which I have now refrained from raising it. The moment in which I chose not to raise my arm is a different moment from the moment I did raise it, and the flow of time in which I chose not to act was not the same as the past flow of time in which I acted. Even if I imagine an action in the very earliest moment of the present, unevoked by any cause, the infinitesimal instant of the present as it becomes the past would still contain a minimum of necessity.

365.11.oldText: Just as in astronomy the difficulty of recognizing the motion of the earth lay in abandoning the immediate sensation of the earth's stability and the planets' apparent motion, so in history the difficulty of recognizing the subjection of the individual to the laws of space, time, and cause lies in abandoning the immediate feeling of the independence of one's own personality.

9.46.oldText: "Bravo! Well done! Now that's a bet! Unbelievable!" came the shouts from all sides.

32.110.oldText: "Yes, it's a nice purse... yes, yes," he said, suddenly turning pale. "Take a look, young man."

38.11.oldText: [Speaking in French] "However, my dear fellow," he remarked, examining his nails from a distance and puckering the skin above his left eye, "despite the deep respect I hold for the Orthodox Russian army, I must confess that your victory was not exactly the most victorious of victories."

45.0.oldText: Remounting his horse, Prince Andrew lingered by the battery, watching the puff of smoke from the gun that had fired the shot. His eyes swept rapidly across the broad field, and he could see that the previously motionless French masses had begun to stir, and that there really was a battery on their left. The smoke from it hadn't yet cleared before another puff appeared, followed by the boom of a cannon. The battle had begun. Prince Andrew wheeled his horse around and galloped back to Grunth to find Prince Bagration. Behind him, the cannonade was growing louder and more frequent. Clearly, the Russian guns had started firing back. From the low ground where the parley had taken place that morning came the crackle of musket fire.

51.5.oldText: On Hélène's name day, a small gathering of 'just family'—as his wife put it—assembled for supper at Prince Vasili's. All these friends and relatives had been given to understand that the young woman's fate would be decided that evening. The guests took their seats at supper. Princess Kuragina, a stout, imposing woman who had once been beautiful, sat at the head of the table. On either side of her were the most important guests—an old general and his wife, and Anna Pavlovna Scherer. At the other end sat the younger and less important guests, along with family members, and there too sat Pierre and Hélène, side by side. Prince Vasili wasn't eating supper; he circled the table in high spirits, sitting down with one guest after another and making casual, pleasant remarks to each—except to Pierre and Hélène, whose presence he seemed not to notice. He kept the whole party lively. The wax candles burned brightly; the silver and crystal gleamed, as did the ladies' gowns and the gold and silver of the men's epaulettes. Servants in scarlet livery moved around the table; the clatter of plates, knives, and glasses blended with the animated buzz of several conversations. At one end, an old chamberlain was assuring an old baroness of his passionate love for her, at which she laughed. At the other end, someone was telling the story of some poor Mary Viktorovna's misfortunes. In the center, Prince Vasili held everyone's attention. With a playful smile, he was telling the ladies about last Wednesday's meeting of the Imperial Council, at which Sergei Kuzmich Vyazminitov, the new military governor general of Petersburg, had received and read the now-famous letter from Emperor Alexander to Sergei Kuzmich. In it, the Emperor said he was receiving declarations of loyalty from all sides, that the one from Petersburg gave him special pleasure, and that he was proud to lead such a nation and would strive to be worthy of it. The letter began: 'Sergei Kuzmich, From all sides reports reach me...' and so on.

56.51.oldText: "Would you believe it, Count — I wasn't the least bit nervous, because I knew I was in the right. Without meaning to boast, I can say that I know the Army Regulations by heart, as well as I know the Lord's Prayer. So there's never any sloppiness in my company, and my conscience was clear. I stepped forward..." Berg stood up to demonstrate how he'd presented himself, hand at his cap, and it would have been hard to find a face expressing greater self-respect and self-satisfaction. "Well, he stormed at me — stormed and stormed and stormed! It wasn't about life so much as death, as the saying goes. 'Albanians!' and 'devils!' and 'off to Siberia!'" Berg said with a knowing smile. "I knew I was right, so I kept quiet. Wasn't that the best approach, Count? 'Hey, are you deaf?' he yelled. I still said nothing. And guess what, Count? The next day there wasn't a word about it in the daily orders. That's what keeping your head gets you. That's how it's done, Count," Berg concluded, lighting his pipe and blowing smoke rings.

60.7.oldText: Just as in a clock's mechanism, so in the mechanism of the military machine: once an impulse is given, it leads inevitably to the final result. And just as the untouched parts of a clock sit completely still until the motion reaches them — wheels that could remain idle for a hundred years — so it is in an army. But the moment comes when the lever catches, and that dormant wheel begins to creak and joins the common motion, the ultimate result and purpose of which are beyond its comprehension.

98.5.oldText: "I've known you a long time, you see, and love you like a brother," she said. "How do you find Andrew?" she added quickly, not giving him time to respond to her warm words. "I'm very worried about him. His health was better in winter, but last spring his wound reopened and the doctor said he should go away for treatment. And I'm also very much afraid for him spiritually. He doesn't have a temperament like us women, who can cry away our sorrows. He keeps everything locked inside. Today he's cheerful and in good spirits — but that's the effect of your visit; he's not often like this. If you could persuade him to go abroad... He needs activity, and this quiet, routine life is very bad for him. Others don't notice it, but I see it."

116.5.oldText: I got up late. On waking I lay in bed a long time, giving in to laziness. O God, help and strengthen me that I may walk in Your ways! Read the Scriptures, but without proper feeling. Afterward went and paced up and down the large hall. I wanted to meditate, but instead my imagination kept returning to something that happened four years ago, when Dolokhov, meeting me in Moscow after our duel, said he hoped I was enjoying perfect peace of mind despite my wife's absence. At the time I gave him no answer. Now I replayed every detail of that meeting and in my mind gave him the most vicious and bitter replies. I caught myself and drove away that thought only when I realized I was burning with anger — but I did not repent enough. Afterward Boris Drubetskoy came and began telling various stories. His visit irritated me from the start, and I said something unpleasant to him. He responded. I lost my temper and said much that was rude and even cruel to him. He fell silent, and I only came to my senses when it was too late. My God, I simply cannot get along with him. The reason is my own selfishness. I put myself above him and so become much worse than he is, for he is patient with my rudeness while I harbor contempt for him. O God, grant that in his presence I may instead see my own failings, and behave so that he too may benefit. After dinner I fell asleep, and as I was dozing off I clearly heard a voice in my left ear saying: "Your day!"

150.6.oldText: Death gives relief and death is peaceful. Ah! From suffering there is no other refuge.

150.11.oldText: Poisonous nourishment of a too sensitive soul, Thou, without whom happiness would be impossible for me, Tender melancholy, ah, come and console me, Come calm the torments of my gloomy retreat, And mingle a secret sweetness with these tears that I feel flowing.

155.5.oldText: While saying this he never took his smiling eyes off her face, her neck, and her bare arms. Natasha knew for certain that he was captivated by her. This pleased her, yet his presence made her feel constrained and uneasy. When she wasn't looking at him she felt that he was looking at her shoulders, and she involuntarily caught his eye so that he would look into her eyes rather than at her body. But looking into his eyes she was frightened, realizing that the barrier of modesty she had always felt between herself and other men didn't exist between them. She didn't know how it was that within five minutes she had come to feel terrifyingly close to this man. They spoke of the most ordinary things, yet she felt that they were closer than she had ever been to any man. Natasha kept turning to Helene and to her father, as if asking what it all meant, but Helene was engaged in conversation with a general and didn't return her look, and her father's eyes said nothing but what they always said: "Having a good time? Well, I'm glad of it!"

158.0.oldText: Count Rostov took the girls to Countess Bezukhova's. There were a good many people there, but nearly all strangers to Natasha. Count Rostov was displeased to see that the company consisted almost entirely of men and women known for the looseness of their behavior. Mademoiselle George was standing in a corner of the drawing room surrounded by young men. There were several Frenchmen present, among them Metivier, who from the time Helene reached Moscow had been a regular in her house. The count decided not to sit down to cards or let his girls out of his sight and to leave as soon as Mademoiselle George's performance was over.

158.1.oldText: Anatole was at the door, obviously on the lookout for the Rostovs. Immediately after greeting the count, he went up to Natasha and followed her. As soon as she saw him she was seized by the same feeling she had had at the opera — a gratified vanity at his admiration and fear at the absence of any moral barrier between them.

158.2.oldText: Helene welcomed Natasha with delight and was loud in her admiration of her beauty and her dress. Soon after their arrival, Mademoiselle George went out to change her costume. In the drawing room people began arranging chairs and taking their seats. Anatole moved a chair for Natasha and was about to sit down beside her, but the count, who never lost sight of her, took the seat himself. Anatole sat down behind her.

158.3.oldText: Mademoiselle George, with her bare, plump, dimpled arms and a red shawl draped over one shoulder, came into the space left for her and struck an unnatural pose. Enthusiastic whispering was audible.

158.4.oldText: Mademoiselle George looked sternly and gloomily at the audience and began reciting some French verses describing her guilty love for her son. In some places she raised her voice, in others she whispered, lifting her head triumphantly; sometimes she paused and uttered hoarse sounds, rolling her eyes.

158.5.oldText: "Adorable! Divine! Delicious!" was heard from every side.

158.6.oldText: Natasha looked at the plump actress, but neither saw nor heard nor understood anything of what was going on before her. She only felt herself once again completely carried away into this strange, senseless world — so far removed from her old life — a world in which it was impossible to tell what was good or bad, reasonable or senseless. Behind her sat Anatole, and conscious of his nearness she felt a frightened sense of anticipation.

158.7.oldText: After the first monologue the whole company rose and surrounded Mademoiselle George, expressing their enthusiasm.

158.8.oldText: "How beautiful she is!" Natasha remarked to her father, who had also gotten up and was moving through the crowd toward the actress.

158.9.oldText: "I don't think so when I look at you!" said Anatole, following Natasha. He said this at a moment when only she could hear him. "You are enchanting... from the moment I saw you I have never ceased..."

158.10.oldText: "Come, come, Natasha!" said the count, turning back for his daughter. "How beautiful she is!" Natasha, without saying anything, stepped up to her father and looked at him with surprised, questioning eyes.

158.11.oldText: After giving several recitations, Mademoiselle George left, and Countess Bezukhova invited her guests into the ballroom.

158.12.oldText: The count wanted to go home, but Helene begged him not to spoil her impromptu ball, and the Rostovs stayed. Anatole asked Natasha for a waltz, and as they danced he pressed her waist and hand and told her she was bewitching and that he loved her. During the ecossaise, which she also danced with him, Anatole said nothing when they happened to be alone, but simply gazed at her. Natasha lifted her frightened eyes to him, but there was such confident tenderness in his affectionate look and smile that she could not, while looking at him, say what she needed to say. She lowered her eyes.

158.13.oldText: "Don't say such things to me. I'm engaged and I love another," she said quickly... She glanced at him.

158.14.oldText: Anatole was not upset or hurt by what she had said.

158.15.oldText: "Don't talk to me about that! What can I do?" said he. "I tell you I'm madly, madly, in love with you! Is it my fault that you are enchanting?... It's our turn to begin."

158.16.oldText: Natasha, excited and bewildered, looked around with wide, frightened eyes and seemed merrier than usual. She understood hardly anything that went on that evening. They danced the ecossaise and the Grossvater. Her father asked her to come home, but she begged to stay. Wherever she went and whomever she was talking to, she felt his eyes upon her. Later she recalled how she had asked her father to let her go to the dressing room to fix her dress, that Helene had followed her and spoken laughingly of her brother's love, and that she met Anatole again in the small sitting room. Helene had disappeared, leaving them alone, and Anatole had taken her hand and said in a tender voice:

158.17.oldText: "I cannot come to visit you, but is it possible that I shall never see you? I love you madly. Can I never...?" and, blocking her path, he brought his face close to hers.

158.18.oldText: His large, glittering, masculine eyes were so close to hers that she saw nothing but them.

158.19.oldText: "Natalie?" he whispered questioningly while she felt her hands being painfully squeezed. "Natalie?"

158.21.oldText: Burning lips were pressed to hers, and at the same instant she felt herself released, and Helene's footsteps and the rustle of her dress were heard in the room. Natasha looked around at her, and then, red and trembling, threw a frightened look of inquiry at Anatole and moved toward the door.

158.23.oldText: She paused. She so needed a word from him that would explain what had happened and to which she could find no answer.

158.24.oldText: "Natalie, just a word, only one!" he kept repeating, clearly not knowing what to say, and he repeated it until Helene came up to them.

158.25.oldText: Helene returned with Natasha to the drawing room. The Rostovs left without staying for supper.

158.26.oldText: After reaching home, Natasha did not sleep all night. She was tormented by the unanswerable question of whether she loved Anatole or Prince Andrew. She loved Prince Andrew — she remembered distinctly how deeply she loved him. But she also loved Anatole — of that there was no doubt. "Otherwise, how could all this have happened?" she thought. "If, after that, I could return his smile when saying goodbye, if I was able to let it come to that, it means I loved him from the first. It means he is kind, noble, and wonderful, and I couldn't help loving him. What am I to do if I love him and the other one too?" she asked herself, unable to find an answer to these terrible questions.

168.0.oldText: From the end of 1811, an intensified buildup and concentration of the forces of Western Europe began, and in 1812 these forces — millions of men, counting those transporting and feeding the army — moved from the west eastward to the Russian frontier, toward which since 1811 Russian forces had been similarly drawn. On June twelfth, 1812, the forces of Western Europe crossed the Russian frontier and war began — that is, an event took place contrary to human reason and to human nature. Millions of men committed against one another such innumerable crimes, frauds, betrayals, thefts, forgeries, counterfeiting, robberies, arson, and murders as in whole centuries are not recorded in the annals of all the law courts of the world, but which those who committed them did not at the time regard as crimes.

168.1.oldText: What produced this extraordinary event? What were its causes? The historians tell us with naive assurance that its causes were the wrongs inflicted on the Duke of Oldenburg, the failure to observe the Continental System, the ambition of Napoleon, the firmness of Alexander, the mistakes of the diplomats, and so on.

168.2.oldText: Consequently, it would only have been necessary for Metternich, Rumyantsev, or Talleyrand, between a reception and a dinner party, to have taken proper pains and written a more skillful note, or for Napoleon to have written to Alexander: "My respected Brother, I consent to restore the duchy to the Duke of Oldenburg" — and there would have been no war.

168.3.oldText: We can understand that the matter appeared that way to contemporaries. It naturally seemed to Napoleon that the war was caused by England's intrigues (as in fact he said on the island of St. Helena). It naturally seemed to members of the English Parliament that the cause of the war was Napoleon's ambition; to the Duke of Oldenburg, that the cause was the violence done to him; to businessmen, that the cause was the Continental System which was ruining Europe; to the generals and old soldiers, that the main reason for the war was the necessity of giving them employment; to the legitimists of that day, that it was the need of restoring good principles; and to the diplomats, that it all resulted from the fact that the alliance between Russia and Austria in 1809 had not been sufficiently well concealed from Napoleon, and from the clumsy wording of Memorandum No. 178. It is natural that these and a countless number of other reasons — the number depending on the endless diversity of viewpoints — presented themselves to the people of that day; but to us, to posterity, who view the event in all its magnitude and perceive its plain and terrible meaning, these causes seem inadequate. To us it is incomprehensible that millions of Christian men killed and tortured each other either because Napoleon was ambitious or Alexander was firm, or because England's policy was astute or the Duke of Oldenburg was wronged. We cannot grasp what connection such circumstances have with the actual fact of slaughter and violence: why, because the Duke was wronged, thousands of men from the other side of Europe killed and ruined the people of Smolensk and Moscow and were killed by them.

168.4.oldText: To us, their descendants, who are not historians and are not swept up in the process of research and can therefore view the event with unclouded common sense, an incalculable number of causes present themselves. The deeper we delve in search of these causes, the more of them we find; and each separate cause or whole series of causes appears to us equally valid in itself and equally false in its insignificance compared to the magnitude of the events, and in its powerlessness — apart from the cooperation of all the other coinciding causes — to produce the event. To us, the wish or objection of this or that French corporal to serve a second term appears as much a cause as Napoleon's refusal to withdraw his troops beyond the Vistula and to restore the duchy of Oldenburg; for had he not wished to serve, and had a second, a third, and a thousandth corporal and private also refused, there would have been so many fewer men in Napoleon's army and the war could not have occurred.

168.5.oldText: Had Napoleon not taken offense at the demand that he should withdraw beyond the Vistula, and not ordered his troops to advance, there would have been no war; but had all his sergeants objected to serving a second term, there could have been no war either. Nor could there have been a war had there been no English intrigues and no Duke of Oldenburg, and had Alexander not felt insulted, and had there not been an autocratic government in Russia, or a Revolution in France and a subsequent dictatorship and Empire, or all the things that produced the French Revolution, and so on. Without each of these causes nothing could have happened. So all these causes — myriads of causes — combined to bring it about. And so there was no single cause for that event, but it had to occur because it had to. Millions of men, abandoning their human feelings and reason, had to march from west to east to slay their fellows, just as some centuries earlier hordes of men had come from the east to the west, slaying their fellows.

168.6.oldText: The actions of Napoleon and Alexander, on whose words the event seemed to depend, were as little voluntary as the actions of any soldier drawn into the campaign by lot or by conscription. This could not be otherwise, for in order that the will of Napoleon and Alexander (on whom the event seemed to depend) should be carried out, the agreement of innumerable circumstances was needed, without any one of which the event could not have taken place. It was necessary that millions of men in whose hands lay the real power — the soldiers who fired, or transported provisions and guns — should consent to carry out the will of these weak individuals, and should have been induced to do so by an infinite number of diverse and complex causes.

168.7.oldText: We are forced to fall back on fatalism as an explanation of irrational events (that is, events whose reasonableness we do not understand). The more we try to explain such events in history rationally, the more unreasonable and incomprehensible they become to us.

168.8.oldText: Each man lives for himself, using his freedom to achieve his personal aims, and feels with his whole being that he can now do or refrain from doing this or that action; but as soon as he has done it, that action performed at a certain moment in time becomes irrevocable and belongs to history, in which it has not a free but a predetermined significance.

168.9.oldText: There are two sides to the life of every man: his individual life, which is the more free the more abstract its interests, and his elemental hive life in which he inevitably obeys laws laid down for him.

168.10.oldText: Man lives consciously for himself, but serves as an unconscious instrument in the attainment of the historic, universal aims of humanity. A deed done is irrevocable, and its result, coinciding in time with the actions of millions of other men, takes on historic significance. The higher a man stands on the social ladder, the more people he is connected with and the more power he has over others, the more obvious is the predestination and inevitability of his every action.

168.13.oldText: History — that is, the unconscious, general, hive life of mankind — uses every moment of the life of kings as a tool for its own purposes.

168.14.oldText: Though Napoleon at that time, in 1812, was more convinced than ever that it depended on him whether to shed (or not to shed) the blood of his peoples — as Alexander expressed it in the last letter he wrote him — he had never been so much in the grip of inevitable laws, which compelled him, while thinking that he was acting on his own free will, to perform for the hive life — that is, for history — whatever had to be performed.

168.15.oldText: (The French phrase means: "To shed (or not to shed) the blood of his peoples.")

168.16.oldText: The people of the west moved eastward to slay their fellow men, and by the law of coincidence thousands of minute causes aligned and combined to produce that movement and war: complaints about the failure to observe the Continental System, the Duke of Oldenburg's wrongs, the movement of troops into Prussia — undertaken (as it seemed to Napoleon) solely to secure an armed peace, the French Emperor's love and habit of war coinciding with his people's inclinations, the allure of the grand preparations, and the expenditure on those preparations and the need to recoup them, the intoxicating honors he received in Dresden, the diplomatic negotiations which contemporaries believed were conducted with a sincere desire for peace but which only wounded the pride of both sides, and millions of other causes that adapted themselves to the event or coincided with it.

168.17.oldText: When an apple has ripened and falls, why does it fall? Because of its attraction to the earth, because its stalk withers, because it is dried by the sun, because it grows heavier, because the wind shakes it, or because the boy standing below wants to eat it?

168.18.oldText: Nothing is the cause. All this is merely the coincidence of conditions in which all vital organic and elemental events occur. And the botanist who finds that the apple falls because the cellular tissue decays and so forth is equally right with the child who stands under the tree and says the apple fell because he wanted to eat it and prayed for it. Equally right or wrong is he who says Napoleon went to Moscow because he wanted to, and perished because Alexander desired his destruction, and he who says that an undermined hill weighing a million tons fell because the last laborer struck it for the last time with his pickaxe. In historic events, the so-called great men are labels giving names to events, and like labels they have only the smallest connection with the event itself.

168.19.oldText: Every act of theirs, which appears to them an act of their own will, is in a historical sense involuntary and is related to the whole course of history and predetermined from eternity.

169.0.oldText: On the twenty-ninth of May Napoleon left Dresden, where he had spent three weeks surrounded by a court that included princes, dukes, kings, and even an emperor. Before leaving, Napoleon showed favor to the emperor, kings, and princes who had earned it, scolded the kings and princes he was displeased with, presented pearls and diamonds of his own — that is, those he had taken from other kings — to the Empress of Austria, and having, as his historian tells us, tenderly embraced the Empress Marie Louise — who regarded him as her husband, though he had left another wife in Paris — left her grieved by the parting which she seemed hardly able to bear. Though the diplomats still firmly believed in the possibility of peace and worked hard to that end, and though Emperor Napoleon himself wrote a letter to Alexander calling him Monsieur mon frere and sincerely assuring him that he did not want war and would always love and honor him — yet he set off to join his army, and at every station gave fresh orders to speed up the movement of his troops from west to east. He traveled in a coach with six horses, surrounded by pages, aides-de-camp, and an escort, along the road to Posen, Thorn, Danzig, and Konigsberg. At each of these towns thousands of people met him with excitement and enthusiasm.

169.1.oldText: The army was moving from west to east, and relays of six horses carried him in the same direction. On June tenth, coming up with the army, he spent the night in quarters prepared for him on the estate of a Polish count in the Vilkavisski forest.

169.3.oldText: Next day, overtaking the army, he went in a carriage to the Niemen, and changing into a Polish uniform, drove to the riverbank to select a place for the crossing.

169.4.oldText: Seeing on the other side some Cossacks and the wide-spreading steppes in the midst of which lay the holy city of Moscow, the capital of a realm such as the Scythia into which Alexander the Great had marched — Napoleon unexpectedly, and contrary alike to strategic and diplomatic considerations, ordered an advance, and the next day his army began to cross the Niemen.

169.5.oldText: Early in the morning of June twelfth, he came out of his tent, which was pitched that day on the steep left bank of the Niemen, and looked through a spyglass at the streams of his troops pouring out of the Vilkavisski forest and flowing over the three bridges thrown across the river. The troops, knowing of the Emperor's presence, were on the lookout for him, and when they caught sight of a figure in an overcoat and a cocked hat standing apart from his suite in front of his tent on the hill, they threw up their caps and shouted: "Vive l'Empereur!" and one after another poured in a ceaseless stream out of the vast forest that had concealed them and, splitting apart, flowed on and on across the three bridges to the other side.

169.6.oldText: "Now we'll get into action. Oh, when he takes it in hand himself, things get hot... by heaven!... There he is!... Vive l'Empereur! So these are the steppes of Asia! It's a miserable country all the same. Goodbye, Beauche — I'll save the best palace in Moscow for you! Goodbye. Good luck!... Did you see the Emperor? Vive l'Empereur!... If they make me Governor of India, Gerard, I'll make you Minister of Kashmir — that's settled. Vive l'Empereur! Hurrah! hurrah! hurrah! The Cossacks — those rascals — see how they run! Vive l'Empereur! There he is, do you see him? I've seen him twice, as I see you now. The little corporal... I saw him give the cross to one of the veterans... Vive l'Empereur!" came the voices of men, old and young, of the most diverse characters and social positions. On the faces of all was one common expression of joy at the start of the long-expected campaign and of adoration and devotion to the man in the gray coat who was standing on the hill.

169.7.oldText: On June thirteenth, a rather small, thoroughbred Arab horse was brought to Napoleon. He mounted it and rode at a gallop to one of the bridges over the Niemen, deafened by constant rapturous cheering which he clearly endured only because it was impossible to forbid the soldiers from expressing their love for him this way, but which disturbed him and distracted him from the military concerns that had occupied him from the moment he joined the army. He rode across one of the swaying pontoon bridges to the other side, turned sharply to the left, and galloped toward Kovno, preceded by mounted chasseurs of the Guard who, breathless with delight, galloped ahead to clear a path for him through the troops. On reaching the broad river Viliya, he stopped near a regiment of Polish Uhlans stationed by the river.

169.8.oldText: "Vivat!" shouted the Poles ecstatically, breaking their ranks and pressing against one another to see him.

169.9.oldText: Napoleon looked up and down the river, dismounted, and sat down on a log lying on the bank. At a silent signal from him, a telescope was handed to him, which he rested on the back of a happy page who had run up, and he gazed at the opposite bank. Then he became absorbed in a map laid out on the logs. Without lifting his head, he said something, and two of his aides-de-camp galloped off to the Polish Uhlans.

169.10.oldText: "What? What did he say?" was heard in the ranks of the Polish Uhlans when one of the aides-de-camp rode up to them.

169.11.oldText: The order was to find a ford and cross the river. The colonel of the Polish Uhlans, a handsome old man, flushed and stammering with excitement, asked the aide-de-camp whether he would be permitted to swim the river with his Uhlans instead of looking for a ford. In obvious fear of refusal, like a boy asking permission to ride a horse, he begged to be allowed to swim across before the Emperor's eyes. The aide-de-camp replied that probably the Emperor would not be displeased by this excess of zeal.

169.12.oldText: As soon as the aide-de-camp said this, the old mustachioed officer, his face glowing with happiness and his eyes sparkling, raised his saber, shouted "Vivat!" and commanding the Uhlans to follow him, spurred his horse and galloped into the river. He gave an angry kick to his horse, which had grown restive, and plunged into the water, heading for the deepest part where the current was swift. Hundreds of Uhlans galloped in after him. It was cold and frightening in the swift current in the middle of the stream, and the Uhlans grabbed at one another as they fell off their horses. Some of the horses drowned and some of the men; the others tried to swim on, some in the saddle and some clinging to their horses' manes. They tried to reach the opposite bank and, though there was a ford a third of a mile away, were proud that they were swimming and drowning in this river under the eyes of the man who sat on the log and wasn't even looking at what they were doing. When the aide-de-camp, having returned and choosing an opportune moment, dared to draw the Emperor's attention to the devotion of the Poles to his person, the little man in the gray overcoat got up and, having summoned Berthier, began pacing up and down the bank with him, giving him instructions and occasionally glancing disapprovingly at the drowning Uhlans who were distracting his attention.

169.13.oldText: For him it was no new conviction that his presence in any part of the world, from Africa to the steppes of Russia alike, was enough to overwhelm people and drive them to insane self-sacrifice. He called for his horse and rode to his quarters.

169.14.oldText: Some forty Uhlans drowned in the river, though boats were sent to help them. The majority struggled back to the bank from which they had started. The colonel and some of his men got across and with difficulty scrambled out on the far bank. And as soon as they had gotten out, in their soaked and streaming clothes, they shouted "Vivat!" and gazed ecstatically at the spot where Napoleon had been but where he no longer was — and at that moment considered themselves happy.

169.15.oldText: That evening, between issuing one order that the counterfeit Russian paper money prepared for use in Russia should be delivered as quickly as possible and another that a Saxon should be shot on whom a letter had been found containing information about French army orders, Napoleon also gave instructions that the Polish colonel who had needlessly plunged into the river should be enrolled in the Legion of Honor, of which Napoleon was himself the head.

169.17.oldText: ("Those whom God wishes to destroy, He first drives mad.")

170.0.oldText: The Emperor of Russia had meanwhile been in Vilna for more than a month, reviewing troops and holding maneuvers. Nothing was ready for the war that everyone expected and to prepare for which the Emperor had come from Petersburg. There was no general plan of action. The uncertainty about the various plans that had been proposed had only increased after the Emperor had spent a month at headquarters. Each of the three armies had its own commander in chief, but there was no supreme commander of all the forces, and the Emperor did not take on that responsibility himself.

170.1.oldText: The longer the Emperor stayed in Vilna, the less did everyone — tired of waiting — prepare for the war. All the efforts of those surrounding the sovereign seemed aimed merely at making him spend his time pleasantly and forget that war was looming.

170.2.oldText: In June, after many balls and celebrations given by the Polish magnates, by the courtiers, and by the Emperor himself, it occurred to one of the Polish aides-de-camp in attendance that a dinner and ball should be given for the Emperor by his aides-de-camp. This idea was eagerly received. The Emperor gave his consent. The aides-de-camp collected money by subscription. The lady thought most likely to please the Emperor was invited to act as hostess. Count Bennigsen, being a landowner in the Vilna province, offered his country house for the occasion, and June thirteenth was fixed for a ball, dinner, boat race, and fireworks at Zakret, Count Bennigsen's country estate.

170.3.oldText: The very day that Napoleon issued the order to cross the Niemen, and his vanguard drove off the Cossacks and crossed the Russian frontier, Alexander spent the evening at the party given by his aides-de-camp at Bennigsen's country house.

170.4.oldText: It was a gay and brilliant celebration. Connoisseurs declared that rarely had so many beautiful women been assembled in one place. Countess Bezukhova was present among other Russian ladies who had followed the sovereign from Petersburg to Vilna, and outshone the refined Polish ladies with her impressive, typically Russian beauty. The Emperor noticed her and honored her with a dance.

170.5.oldText: Boris Drubetskoy, having left his wife in Moscow and being for the time being a bachelor (as he put it), was also there and, though not an aide-de-camp, had contributed a large sum toward the expenses. Boris was now a rich man who had risen to high rank and no longer sought patronage but stood on equal footing with the most prominent men of his own age. He was meeting Helene in Vilna after not having seen her for a long time and did not dwell on the past, but as Helene was enjoying the favors of a very important personage and Boris had only recently married, they met as good old friends.

170.6.oldText: At midnight the dancing was still going on. Helene, not having a suitable partner, offered to dance the mazurka with Boris. They were the third couple. Boris, coolly looking at Helene's dazzling bare shoulders which emerged from a dark, gold-embroidered gauze gown, talked to her of old acquaintances and at the same time — unaware of it himself and unnoticed by others — never for an instant stopped watching the Emperor, who was in the same room. The Emperor was not dancing; he stood in the doorway, stopping now one couple and now another with gracious words that he alone knew how to deliver.

170.7.oldText: As the mazurka began, Boris saw that Adjutant General Balashev, one of those closest to the Emperor, went up to him and — contrary to court etiquette — stood near him while he was talking to a Polish lady. Having finished speaking to her, the Emperor looked inquiringly at Balashev and, evidently understanding that he acted this way only because there were important reasons for doing so, gave a slight nod to the lady and turned to Balashev. Hardly had Balashev begun to speak before a look of amazement appeared on the Emperor's face. He took Balashev by the arm and crossed the room with him, unconsciously clearing a path seven yards wide as people on both sides made way for him. Boris noticed Arakcheev's agitated face when the sovereign left with Balashev. Arakcheev looked at the Emperor from under his brow and, sniffing with his red nose, stepped forward from the crowd as if expecting the Emperor to address him. (Boris understood that Arakcheev envied Balashev and was displeased that evidently important news had reached the Emperor through someone other than himself.)

170.8.oldText: But the Emperor and Balashev passed out into the illuminated garden without noticing Arakcheev, who, holding his sword and glancing angrily around, followed about twenty paces behind them.

170.9.oldText: All the time Boris was going through the figures of the mazurka, he was preoccupied with the question of what news Balashev had brought and how he could find it out before others. In the figure where he had to choose two ladies, he whispered to Helene that he meant to choose Countess Potocka who, he thought, had gone out onto the veranda, and glided across the parquet toward the door opening into the garden, where, seeing Balashev and the Emperor returning to the veranda, he stopped. They were moving toward the door. Boris, fluttering as if he hadn't had time to withdraw, respectfully pressed close to the doorpost with bowed head.

170.10.oldText: The Emperor, with the agitation of a man who has been personally offended, was finishing with these words:

170.11.oldText: "To enter Russia without declaring war! I will not make peace as long as a single armed enemy remains on my soil!" It seemed to Boris that it gave the Emperor pleasure to utter these words. He was satisfied with the way he had expressed his thoughts but displeased that Boris had overheard them.

170.13.oldText: Boris understood that this was meant for him and, closing his eyes, slightly bowed his head. The Emperor re-entered the ballroom and stayed about another half hour.

170.14.oldText: Boris was thus the first to learn that the French army had crossed the Niemen, and thanks to this was able to show certain important personages that much that was hidden from others was usually known to him, and by this means he rose higher in their estimation.

170.15.oldText: The unexpected news of the French having crossed the Niemen was particularly startling after a month of unfulfilled expectations, and at a ball. On first receiving the news, under the influence of outrage and resentment, the Emperor had found a phrase that pleased him, fully expressed his feelings, and has since become famous. On returning home at two o'clock that night he sent for his secretary, Shishkov, and told him to write an order to the troops and a rescript to Field Marshal Prince Saltykov, in which he insisted on the words being included that he would not make peace so long as a single armed Frenchman remained on Russian soil.

170.16.oldText: The next day the following letter was sent to Napoleon:

170.18.oldText: Yesterday I learned that, despite the loyalty with which I have kept my commitments to Your Majesty, your troops have crossed the Russian frontier, and I have this moment received from Petersburg a note in which Count Lauriston states, as a reason for this aggression, that Your Majesty has considered yourself to be in a state of war with me from the time Prince Kurakin asked for his passports. The reasons on which the Duc de Bassano based his refusal to deliver them to him would never have led me to suppose that could serve as a pretext for aggression. In fact, the ambassador, as he himself has declared, was never authorized to make that demand, and as soon as I was informed of it I let him know how much I disapproved of it and ordered him to remain at his post. If Your Majesty does not intend to shed the blood of our peoples for such a misunderstanding, and consents to withdraw your troops from Russian territory, I will regard what has passed as not having occurred and an understanding between us will be possible. In the contrary case, Your Majesty, I shall see myself forced to repel an attack that nothing on my part has provoked. It still depends on Your Majesty to preserve humanity from the calamity of another war.

173.0.oldText: Though Balashev was accustomed to imperial magnificence, he was amazed at the luxury and splendor of Napoleon's court.

173.1.oldText: The Count de Turenne showed him into a large reception room where many generals, gentlemen-in-waiting, and Polish magnates — several of whom Balashev had seen at the court of the Emperor of Russia — were waiting. Duroc said that Napoleon would receive the Russian general before going for his ride.

173.2.oldText: After some minutes, the gentleman-in-waiting on duty came into the great reception room and, bowing politely, asked Balashev to follow him.

173.3.oldText: Balashev went into a small reception room, one door of which led into a study — the very one from which the Russian Emperor had dispatched him on his mission. He stood a minute or two, waiting. He heard hurried footsteps beyond the door, both halves of it were opened rapidly; all was silent, and then from the study came the sound of other steps, firm and resolute — those of Napoleon. He had just finished dressing for his ride and wore a blue uniform, opening in front over a white waistcoat so long that it covered his round stomach, white leather breeches tightly fitting the plump thighs of his short legs, and Hessian boots. His short hair had obviously just been brushed, but one lock hung down in the middle of his broad forehead. His plump white neck stood out sharply above the black collar of his uniform, and he smelled of cologne. His full face, rather young-looking, with its prominent chin, wore a gracious and majestic expression of imperial welcome.

173.4.oldText: He entered briskly, with a bounce at every step and his head slightly thrown back. His whole short, stout figure, with its broad thick shoulders and chest and stomach naturally jutting forward, had that imposing and stately appearance one sees in well-fed men of forty. It was also evident that he was in the best of spirits that day.

173.5.oldText: He nodded in answer to Balashev's low and respectful bow, and coming up to him at once began speaking like a man who values every moment of his time and does not bother preparing what he has to say, confident that he will always say the right thing and say it well.

173.6.oldText: "Good day, General!" said he. "I have received the letter you brought from the Emperor Alexander and am very glad to see you." He glanced with his large eyes into Balashev's face and immediately looked past him.

173.7.oldText: It was plain that Balashev's personality did not interest him at all. Clearly only what took place within his own mind interested him. Nothing outside himself had any significance for him, because everything in the world, it seemed to him, depended entirely on his will.

173.8.oldText: "I do not, and did not, desire war," he continued, "but it has been forced on me. Even now" (he stressed the word) "I am ready to receive any explanations you can give me."
