273.26.oldText: He turned his head and saw that the adjutant was putting another question to Davout.

273.27.oldText: "Yes, of course!" replied Davout, but what this "yes" meant, Pierre did not know.

273.28.oldText: Pierre could not afterward remember how he went, whether it was far, or in what direction. His faculties were completely numb; he was stupefied, and noticing nothing around him, he went on moving his legs as the others did till they all stopped and he stopped too. The only thought in his mind was: who had really sentenced him to death? Not the men on the commission that had first examined him—not one of them wished to or, evidently, could have done it. It was not Davout, who had looked at him in such a human way. In another moment Davout would have realized that he was doing wrong, but just then the adjutant had come in and interrupted him. The adjutant, too, had evidently had no evil intent, though he might have refrained from coming in. Then who was executing him, killing him, depriving him of life—him, Pierre, with all his memories, aspirations, hopes, and thoughts? Who was doing this? And Pierre felt that it was no one.

273.29.oldText: It was a system—a convergence of circumstances.

273.30.oldText: A system of some sort was killing him—Pierre—depriving him of life, of everything, annihilating him.

274.0.oldText: From Prince Shcherbatov's house the prisoners were led straight down the Virgin's Field, to the left of the nunnery, as far as a kitchen garden where a post had been set up. Beyond that post a fresh pit had been dug in the ground, and near the post and the pit a large crowd stood in a semicircle. The crowd consisted of a few Russians and many of Napoleon's soldiers who were not on duty—Germans, Italians, and Frenchmen, in a variety of uniforms. To the right and left of the post stood rows of French troops in blue uniforms with red epaulets, high boots, and shakos.

274.1.oldText: The prisoners were placed in a certain order, according to the list (Pierre was sixth), and were led to the post. Several drums suddenly began to beat on both sides of them, and at that sound Pierre felt as if part of his soul had been torn away. He lost the power of thinking or understanding. He could only hear and see. And he had only one wish—that the terrible thing that had to happen should happen quickly. Pierre looked round at his fellow prisoners and studied them.

274.2.oldText: The first two were convicts with shaven heads. One was tall and thin, the other dark, shaggy, and sinewy, with a flat nose. The third was a domestic servant, about forty-five years old, with graying hair and a plump, well-nourished body. The fourth was a peasant, a very handsome man with a broad, light-brown beard and black eyes. The fifth was a factory worker, a thin, sallow-faced boy of about eighteen in a loose coat.

274.3.oldText: Pierre heard the French consulting whether to shoot them one at a time or in pairs. "In pairs," replied the officer in command in a calm voice. There was a stir in the ranks of the soldiers, and it was obvious they were all hurrying—not as men hurry to do something they understand, but as people rush to finish a necessary but unpleasant and incomprehensible task.

274.4.oldText: A French official wearing a sash came up to the right of the row of prisoners and read out the sentence in Russian and in French.

274.5.oldText: Then two pairs of Frenchmen approached the condemned men and, at the officer's command, took the two convicts who stood first in the row. The convicts stopped when they reached the post, and while sacks were being brought, looked dumbly around as a wounded beast looks at an approaching hunter. One crossed himself continuously, the other scratched his back and made a movement of the lips resembling a smile. With hurried hands the soldiers blindfolded them, drawing the sacks over their heads, and tied them to the post.

274.6.oldText: Twelve sharpshooters with muskets stepped out of the ranks with a firm, regular tread and halted eight paces from the post. Pierre turned away to avoid seeing what was going to happen. Suddenly a crackling, rolling noise was heard, which seemed to him louder than the most terrific thunder, and he looked around. There was some smoke, and the Frenchmen were doing something near the pit, with pale faces and trembling hands. Two more prisoners were led up. In the same way and with similar looks, these two glanced vainly at the onlookers with only a silent appeal for protection in their eyes, evidently unable to understand or believe what was going to happen to them. They could not believe it because they alone knew what their lives meant to them, and so they neither understood nor believed that those lives could be taken from them.

274.7.oldText: Again Pierre did not wish to look and again turned away; but again the sound of a frightful explosion struck his ear, and at the same moment he saw smoke, blood, and the pale, scared faces of the Frenchmen who were again doing something by the post, their trembling hands getting in one another's way. Pierre, breathing heavily, looked around as if asking what it meant. The same question was expressed in all the faces that met his.

274.8.oldText: On the faces of all the Russians and of the French soldiers and officers without exception, he read the same dismay, horror, and inner conflict that were in his own heart. "But who, after all, is doing this? They are all suffering as I am. Who then is it? Who?" flashed for an instant through his mind.

274.9.oldText: "Sharpshooters of the 86th, forward!" shouted someone. The fifth prisoner, the one next to Pierre, was led away—alone. Pierre did not understand that he was saved, that he and the rest had been brought there only to witness the execution. With ever-growing horror, and no sense of joy or relief, he watched what was happening. The fifth man was the factory boy in the loose coat. The moment they laid hands on him he sprang aside in terror and clutched at Pierre. (Pierre shuddered and shook himself free.) The boy could not walk. They dragged him along, holding him up under the arms, and he screamed. When they got him to the post he grew quiet, as if he suddenly understood something. Whether he understood that screaming was useless, or whether he thought it impossible that men should kill him, he took his stand at the post, waiting to be blindfolded like the others, and like a wounded animal looked around him with glittering eyes.

274.10.oldText: Pierre was no longer able to turn away and close his eyes. His curiosity and agitation, like that of the whole crowd, reached the highest pitch at this fifth murder. Like the others, this fifth man seemed calm; he wrapped his loose coat closer and rubbed one bare foot with the other.

274.11.oldText: When they began to blindfold him, he himself adjusted the knot which hurt the back of his head; then when they propped him against the bloodstained post, he leaned back and, not being comfortable in that position, straightened himself, adjusted his feet, and leaned back again more comfortably. Pierre did not take his eyes from him and did not miss his slightest movement.

274.12.oldText: Probably a word of command was given, followed by the reports of eight muskets; but try as he would, Pierre could not afterwards remember hearing the slightest sound of the shots. He only saw how the worker suddenly sank down on the ropes that held him, how blood appeared in two places, how the ropes slackened under the weight of the hanging body, and how the worker sat down, his head hanging unnaturally and one leg bent under him. Pierre ran up to the post. No one stopped him. Pale, frightened people were doing something around the worker. The lower jaw of an old Frenchman with a thick mustache trembled as he untied the ropes. The body collapsed. The soldiers dragged it awkwardly from the post and began pushing it into the pit.

274.13.oldText: They all plainly and unmistakably knew that they were criminals who must hide the traces of their guilt as quickly as possible.

274.14.oldText: Pierre glanced into the pit and saw that the factory boy was lying with his knees close up to his head and one shoulder higher than the other. That shoulder rose and fell rhythmically and convulsively, but spadefuls of earth were already being thrown over the whole body. One of the soldiers, evidently suffering, shouted gruffly and angrily at Pierre to go back. But Pierre did not understand him and remained near the post, and no one drove him away.

274.15.oldText: When the pit had been filled up, a command was given. Pierre was taken back to his place, and the rows of troops on both sides of the post made a half turn and marched past it at a measured pace. The twenty-four sharpshooters with discharged muskets, standing in the center of the circle, ran back to their places as the companies passed by.

274.16.oldText: Pierre gazed now with dazed eyes at these sharpshooters who ran in pairs out of the circle. All but one rejoined their companies. This one, a young soldier, his face deathly pale, his cap pushed back, and his musket resting on the ground, still stood near the pit at the spot from which he had fired. He swayed like a drunken man, taking some steps forward and back to keep himself from falling. An old noncommissioned officer ran out of the ranks and, taking him by the elbow, dragged him to his company. The crowd of Russians and Frenchmen began to disperse. They all went away silently and with drooping heads.

274.17.oldText: "That will teach them to start fires," said one of the Frenchmen.

274.18.oldText: Pierre glanced at the speaker and saw that it was a soldier who was trying to find some comfort after what had been done, but could not. Without finishing what he had begun to say, he made a hopeless gesture with his arm and went away.

276.0.oldText: Twenty-three soldiers, three officers, and two officials were confined in the shed where Pierre had been placed and where he remained for four weeks.

276.1.oldText: When Pierre remembered them afterward, they all seemed misty figures to him except Platon Karataev, who always remained in his mind the most vivid and precious memory and the embodiment of everything Russian, kindly, and round. When Pierre saw his neighbor the next morning at dawn, the first impression of him—as of something round—was fully confirmed: Platon's whole figure—in a French overcoat belted with a cord, a soldier's cap, and bast shoes—was round. His head was perfectly round, his back, chest, shoulders, and even his arms, which he held as if ever ready to embrace something, were rounded; his pleasant smile and his large, gentle brown eyes were round too.

276.2.oldText: Platon Karataev must have been about fifty, judging by his stories of campaigns he had been in, told like an old soldier. He did not know his own age and was quite unable to determine it. But his brilliantly white, strong teeth—which showed in two unbroken semicircles when he laughed, as he often did—were all sound and good. There was not a gray hair in his beard or on his head, and his whole body gave an impression of suppleness and especially of firmness and endurance.

276.3.oldText: His face, despite its fine, rounded wrinkles, had an expression of innocence and youth; his voice was pleasant and musical. But the chief peculiarity of his speech was its directness and aptness. It was evident that he never considered what he had said or was going to say, and consequently the speed and rightness of his delivery had an irresistible persuasiveness.

276.4.oldText: His physical strength and agility during the first days of his imprisonment were such that he seemed not to know what fatigue and sickness meant. Every night before lying down he said: "Lord, lay me down as a stone and raise me up as a loaf!" And every morning on getting up he said: "I lay down and curled up, I get up and shake myself." And indeed he only had to lie down to fall asleep like a stone, and he only had to shake himself to be ready without a moment's delay for any work, just as children are ready to play the instant they wake. He could do everything—not very well but not badly. He baked, cooked, sewed, planed, and mended boots. He was always busy, and only at night allowed himself conversation—which he loved—and songs. He did not sing like a trained singer who knows he is being listened to, but like the birds, evidently giving vent to the sounds in the same way that one stretches or walks about to relieve stiffness. The sounds were always high-pitched, mournful, delicate, and almost feminine, and his face at such times was very serious.

276.5.oldText: Having been taken prisoner and allowed his beard to grow, he seemed to have thrown off everything that had been forced upon him—everything military and foreign to his nature—and had returned to his former peasant ways.

276.6.oldText: "A soldier on leave—a shirt worn outside the trousers," he would say.

276.7.oldText: He did not like talking about his life as a soldier, though he did not complain, and often mentioned that he had never once been flogged during his whole army service. When he told stories it was generally from old and evidently treasured memories of his "Christian" life, as he called his peasant existence. The proverbs that filled his speech were not the coarse and crude ones soldiers use, but those folk sayings which, taken out of context, seem so insignificant, but which used at the right moment suddenly acquire a significance of profound wisdom.

276.8.oldText: He would often say the exact opposite of what he had said on a previous occasion, yet both would be right. He liked to talk and he talked well, adorning his speech with terms of endearment and folk sayings which Pierre thought he invented himself. But the chief charm of his talk lay in the fact that the most common events—sometimes just such as Pierre had witnessed without taking notice of them—assumed in Karataev's telling a character of solemn meaning. He liked to hear the folk tales one of the soldiers told in the evenings (they were always the same), but most of all he liked to hear stories of real life. He would smile joyfully while listening to such stories, now and then putting in a word or asking a question to make the moral beauty of what he was told clear to himself. Karataev had no attachments, friendships, or love as Pierre understood them, but loved and lived warmly with everything life brought him into contact with, particularly with people—not any particular person, but those with whom he happened to be. He loved his dog, his comrades, the French, and Pierre who was his neighbor; but Pierre felt that despite Karataev's affectionate tenderness for him (by which he unconsciously gave Pierre's spiritual life its due), he would not have grieved for a moment at parting from him. And Pierre began to feel the same way toward Karataev.

276.9.oldText: To all the other prisoners, Platon Karataev seemed a most ordinary soldier. They called him "little falcon" or "Platosha," teased him good-naturedly, and sent him on errands. But to Pierre he always remained what he had seemed that first night: an unfathomable, rounded, eternal personification of the spirit of simplicity and truth.

276.10.oldText: Platon Karataev knew nothing by heart except his prayers. When he began to speak he seemed not to know how he would finish.

276.11.oldText: Sometimes Pierre, struck by the meaning of his words, would ask him to repeat them, but Platon could never recall what he had said a moment before, just as he could never repeat to Pierre the words of his favorite song: native and birch tree and my heart is sick came up in it, but when spoken rather than sung, no meaning could be extracted. He did not, and could not, understand the meaning of words apart from their context. Every word and action of his was the expression of an activity unknown to him, which was his life. But his life, as he saw it, had no meaning as a separate thing. It had meaning only as part of a whole of which he was always conscious. His words and actions flowed from him as evenly, inevitably, and spontaneously as fragrance from a flower. He could not understand the value or significance of any word or deed taken separately.

277.0.oldText: When Princess Mary heard from Nicholas that her brother was with the Rostovs at Yaroslavl, she at once prepared to go there, despite her aunt's efforts to dissuade her—and not merely to go herself but to take her nephew with her. Whether it was difficult or easy, possible or impossible, she did not ask and did not want to know: it was her duty, not only to herself, to be near her brother who was perhaps dying, but to do everything possible to bring his son to him, and so she prepared to set off. That she had not heard from Prince Andrew himself, Princess Mary attributed to his being too weak to write, or to his considering the long journey too hard and too dangerous for her and his son.

277.1.oldText: In a few days Princess Mary was ready to start. Her vehicles were the huge family coach in which she had traveled to Voronezh, a half-open carriage, and a baggage cart. With her traveled Mademoiselle Bourienne, little Nicholas and his tutor, her old nurse, three maids, Tikhon, and a young footman and courier her aunt had sent to accompany her.

277.2.oldText: The usual route through Moscow was out of the question, and the roundabout way Princess Mary was obliged to take through Lipetsk, Ryazan, Vladimir, and Shuya was very long and, since post horses were not available everywhere, very difficult, and near Ryazan—where the French were said to have appeared—even dangerous.

277.3.oldText: During this difficult journey, Mademoiselle Bourienne, Dessalles, and Princess Mary's servants were astonished at her energy and strength of spirit. She went to bed later and rose earlier than any of them, and no difficulties daunted her. Thanks to her activity and energy, which inspired her fellow travelers, they approached Yaroslavl by the end of the second week.

277.4.oldText: The last days of her stay in Voronezh had been the happiest of her life. Her love for Rostov no longer tormented or agitated her. It filled her whole soul, had become an integral part of herself, and she no longer fought against it. She had become convinced that she loved and was loved, though she never said this to herself in words. She had become convinced of it at her last meeting with Nicholas, when he had come to tell her that her brother was with the Rostovs. Not by a single word had Nicholas alluded to the fact that Prince Andrew's relationship with Natasha might, if he recovered, be renewed; but Princess Mary saw from his face that he knew and thought of this.

277.5.oldText: Yet despite that, his attitude toward her—considerate, delicate, and loving—not only remained unchanged, but it sometimes seemed to Princess Mary that he was even glad that the family connection between them allowed him to express his friendship more freely. She knew that she loved for the first and only time in her life, and felt that she was loved, and was happy in that knowledge.

277.6.oldText: But this happiness on one side of her spiritual nature did not prevent her from feeling grief for her brother with full force; on the contrary, that spiritual peace on one side made it all the more possible for her to give full expression to her feeling for her brother. That feeling was so strong at the moment of leaving Voronezh that those who saw her off, looking at her careworn, despairing face, felt certain she would fall ill on the journey. But the very difficulties and demands of the journey, which she took so actively in hand, saved her for a while from her grief and gave her strength.

277.7.oldText: As always happens when traveling, Princess Mary thought only of the journey itself, forgetting its purpose. But as she approached Yaroslavl, the thought of what might await her there—not after many days but that very evening—again presented itself, and her agitation reached its peak.

277.8.oldText: The courier who had been sent ahead to find out where the Rostovs were staying in Yaroslavl and in what condition Prince Andrew was, met the big coach just entering the town gates and was appalled by the terrible pallor of the princess's face looking out at him from the window.

277.9.oldText: "I have found out everything, your excellency: the Rostovs are staying at the merchant Bronnikov's house, in the square not far from here, right above the Volga," said the courier.

277.10.oldText: Princess Mary looked at him with frightened inquiry, not understanding why he did not reply to what she most wanted to know: how was her brother? Mademoiselle Bourienne asked that question for her.

277.12.oldText: "His excellency is staying in the same house with them."

277.13.oldText: "Then he is alive," thought Princess Mary, and asked in a low voice: "How is he?"

277.15.oldText: What "still the same" might mean, Princess Mary did not ask, but with an unnoticed glance at little seven-year-old Nicholas—who was sitting in front of her looking with pleasure at the town—she bowed her head and did not raise it again until the heavy coach, rumbling, shaking, and swaying, came to a stop. The carriage steps clattered as they were let down.

277.16.oldText: The carriage door opened. On the left there was water—a great river—and on the right a porch. There were people at the entrance: servants, and a rosy girl with a large plait of black hair, smiling in a way that seemed to Princess Mary unpleasantly artificial. (This was Sonya.) Princess Mary ran up the steps. "This way, this way!" said the girl with the same artificial smile, and the princess found herself in the hall facing an elderly woman of Eastern appearance, who came quickly toward her with a look of emotion. This was the countess. She embraced Princess Mary and kissed her.

277.17.oldText: "My child!" she murmured, "I love you and have known you a long time."

277.19.oldText: Despite her emotion, Princess Mary realized that this was the countess and that she must say something to her. Hardly knowing how she managed it, she spoke a few polite phrases in French in the same tone as those addressed to her, and asked: "How is he?"

277.20.oldText: "The doctor says he is not in danger," said the countess, but as she spoke she raised her eyes with a sigh, and her gesture conveyed a contradiction of her words.

277.21.oldText: "Where is he? Can I see him—can I?" asked the princess.

277.22.oldText: "One moment, Princess, one moment, my dear! Is this his son?" said the countess, turning to little Nicholas who was coming in with Dessalles. "There will be room for everybody; this is a big house. Oh, what a lovely boy!"

277.23.oldText: The countess took Princess Mary into the drawing room, where Sonya was talking to Mademoiselle Bourienne. The countess caressed the boy, and the old count came in and welcomed the princess. He had changed very much since she had last seen him. Then he had been a brisk, cheerful, self-assured old man; now he seemed a pitiful, bewildered person. While talking to Princess Mary he kept looking around as if asking everyone whether he was doing the right thing. After the destruction of Moscow and of his property, thrown out of his accustomed groove, he seemed to have lost his sense of his own importance and to feel that there was no longer a place for him in life.

277.24.oldText: Despite her one desire to see her brother as soon as possible, and her irritation that at the moment when all she wanted was to see him they were trying to entertain her and pretending to admire her nephew, the princess noticed all that was going on around her and felt the necessity of submitting for a time to this new order of things she had entered. She knew it was necessary, and though it was hard for her, she was not angry with these people.

277.26.oldText: Princess Mary turned to Sonya and, trying to suppress the hostile feeling that arose in her toward the girl, she kissed her. But she felt oppressed by the fact that the mood of everyone around her was so far from what was in her own heart.

277.28.oldText: "He is downstairs. Natasha is with him," answered Sonya, flushing. "We have sent to ask. I think you must be tired, Princess."

277.29.oldText: Tears of frustration showed in Princess Mary's eyes. She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to go to him, when light, eager, and seemingly buoyant steps were heard at the door. The princess looked around and saw Natasha coming in, almost running—that Natasha whom she had liked so little at their meeting in Moscow long before.

277.30.oldText: But hardly had the princess looked at Natasha's face before she realized that here was a true companion in her grief, and therefore a friend. She ran to meet her, embraced her, and began to cry on her shoulder.

277.32.oldText: There was only one expression on her agitated face when she ran into the drawing room—that of love: boundless love for him, for her, and for all that was close to the man she loved; and of pity, suffering for others, and a passionate desire to give herself entirely to helping them. It was plain that at that moment there was in Natasha's heart no thought of herself or of her own relationship with Prince Andrew.

277.33.oldText: Princess Mary, with her acute sensitivity, understood all this at the first glance at Natasha's face, and wept on her shoulder with sorrowful joy.

277.35.oldText: Princess Mary raised her head, dried her eyes, and turned to Natasha. She felt that from her she would be able to understand and learn everything.

277.37.oldText: She felt that it was impossible to ask, or to answer, in words. Natasha's face and eyes would have to tell her everything more clearly and deeply.

277.38.oldText: Natasha was gazing at her but seemed afraid and in doubt whether to say all she knew or not; she seemed to feel that before those luminous eyes that penetrated into the very depths of her heart, it was impossible not to tell the whole truth as she saw it. And suddenly Natasha's lips twitched, ugly wrinkles gathered round her mouth, and covering her face with her hands, she burst into sobs.

277.40.oldText: But she still hoped, and asked in words she herself did not trust:

277.43.oldText: They sat a little while downstairs near his room until they had stopped crying and were able to go to him with calm faces.

277.44.oldText: "How has his whole illness gone? Is it long since he grew worse? When did this happen?" Princess Mary asked.

277.45.oldText: Natasha told her that at first there had been danger from his feverish condition and the pain he suffered, but at Troitsa that had passed and the doctor had only been afraid of gangrene. That danger had also passed. When they reached Yaroslavl, the wound had begun to fester (Natasha knew all about such things as festering), and the doctor had said the festering might take a normal course. Then fever set in, but the doctor had said the fever was not very serious.

278.0.oldText: When Natasha opened Prince Andrew's door with a familiar movement and let Princess Mary pass into the room before her, the princess felt the sobs in her throat. Hard as she had tried to prepare herself and now tried to remain calm, she knew she would be unable to look at him without tears.

278.1.oldText: The princess understood what Natasha had meant by the words: "two days ago this suddenly happened." She understood those words to mean that he had suddenly softened, and that this softening and gentleness were signs of approaching death. As she stepped toward the door she already saw in her imagination Andrew's face as she remembered it in childhood—a gentle, mild, compassionate face which he had rarely shown, and which therefore affected her deeply. She was sure he would speak soft, tender words to her such as her father had said before his death, and that she would not be able to bear it and would burst into sobs in his presence. Yet sooner or later it had to be, and she went in. The sobs rose higher and higher in her throat as she more and more clearly made out his form, and her nearsighted eyes tried to distinguish his features—and then she saw his face and met his gaze.

278.2.oldText: He was lying in a squirrel-fur dressing gown on a divan, surrounded by pillows. He was thin and pale. In one thin, translucently white hand he held a handkerchief, while with the other he slowly stroked the delicate mustache he had grown, moving his fingers slowly. His eyes gazed at them as they entered.

278.3.oldText: On seeing his face and meeting his eyes, Princess Mary's pace suddenly slackened; she felt her tears dry up and her sobs cease. She suddenly felt guilty and grew timid, catching the expression of his face and eyes.

278.4.oldText: "But what am I guilty of?" she asked herself. And his cold, stern look replied: "Because you are alive and thinking of the living, while I..."

278.5.oldText: In the deep gaze that seemed to look not outward but inward, there was an almost hostile expression as he slowly regarded his sister and Natasha.

278.6.oldText: He kissed his sister, holding her hand in his as was their custom.

278.7.oldText: "How are you, Mary? How did you manage to get here?" said he in a voice as calm and detached as his look.

278.8.oldText: Had he screamed in agony, that scream would not have struck such horror into Princess Mary's heart as the tone of his voice.

278.9.oldText: "And have you brought little Nicholas?" he asked in the same slow, quiet manner, with an obvious effort to remember.

278.10.oldText: "How are you now?" said Princess Mary, herself surprised at what she was saying.

278.11.oldText: "That, my dear, you must ask the doctor," he replied, and again making an evident effort to be warm, he said with his lips only (his words clearly did not match his thoughts):

278.14.oldText: Princess Mary pressed his hand. The pressure made him wince just perceptibly. He was silent, and she did not know what to say. She now understood what had happened to him two days before. In his words, his tone, and especially in that calm, almost hostile look could be felt an estrangement from everything belonging to this world—terrible in one who is alive. Evidently only with an effort did he understand anything living; but it was clear that he failed to understand not because he lacked the ability, but because he understood something else—something the living did not and could not understand—and which wholly occupied his mind.

278.15.oldText: "There, you see how strangely fate has brought us together," said he, breaking the silence and pointing to Natasha. "She looks after me all the time."

278.16.oldText: Princess Mary heard him and did not understand how he could say such a thing. He, the sensitive, tender Prince Andrew—how could he say that, in front of the woman he loved and who loved him? Had he expected to live, he could not have spoken those words in that offensively cold tone. If he had not known he was dying, how could he have failed to pity her, and how could he speak like that in her presence? The only explanation was that he was indifferent, because something else, much more important, had been revealed to him.

278.17.oldText: The conversation was cold and disconnected and continually broke off.

278.19.oldText: Prince Andrew did not notice that she called his sister Mary; and only after calling her so in his presence did Natasha notice it herself.

278.21.oldText: "They told her that all Moscow has been burned down, and that..."

278.22.oldText: Natasha stopped. It was impossible to talk. It was plain that he was making an effort to listen but could not.

278.23.oldText: "Yes, they say it's burned," he said. "It's a great pity," and he gazed straight before him, absently stroking his mustache with his fingers.

278.24.oldText: "And so you have met Count Nicholas, Mary?" Prince Andrew suddenly said, evidently wishing to speak pleasantly to them. "He wrote here that he took a great liking to you," he went on simply and calmly, evidently unable to understand all the complex significance his words had for living people. "If you liked him too, it would be a good thing for you to get married," he added rather more quickly, as if pleased at finding words he had long been seeking.

278.25.oldText: Princess Mary heard his words but they had no meaning for her except as proof of how far away he now was from everything living.

278.26.oldText: "Why talk of me?" she said quietly and glanced at Natasha.

278.27.oldText: Natasha, who felt her glance, did not look at her. All three were again silent.

278.28.oldText: "Andrew, would you like..." Princess Mary suddenly said in a trembling voice, "would you like to see little Nicholas? He is always talking about you!"

278.29.oldText: Prince Andrew smiled just perceptibly and for the first time, but Princess Mary, who knew his face so well, saw with horror that he did not smile with pleasure or affection for his son, but with quiet, gentle irony—because he thought she was trying what she believed to be the last means of rousing him.

278.30.oldText: "Yes, I shall be very glad to see him. Is he quite well?"

278.32.oldText: When Nicholas had been led away, Princess Mary again went up to her brother, kissed him, and unable to hold back her tears any longer, began to cry.

278.35.oldText: Princess Mary nodded her head, weeping.

278.39.oldText: When Princess Mary began to cry, he understood that she was crying at the thought that little Nicholas would be left without a father. With a great effort he tried to return to life and to see things from their point of view.

278.41.oldText: "The birds of the air neither sow nor reap, yet your Father feeds them," he said to himself, and wished to say to Princess Mary; "but no, they will take it their own way. They won't understand! They can't understand that all those feelings they prize so—all our feelings, all those ideas that seem so important to us—are unnecessary. We cannot understand one another." And he remained silent.

278.42.oldText: Prince Andrew's little son was seven. He could scarcely read and knew nothing. After that day he lived through many things, gaining knowledge, observation, and experience; but had he possessed all the faculties he later acquired, he could not have had a better or more profound understanding of the meaning of the scene he had witnessed between his father, Mary, and Natasha than he had then. He understood it completely, and leaving the room without crying, went silently up to Natasha—who had come out with him—and looked shyly at her with his beautiful, thoughtful eyes. Then his upturned, rosy upper lip trembled, and leaning his head against her, he began to cry.

278.43.oldText: After that he avoided Dessalles and the countess who caressed him, and either sat alone or came timidly to Princess Mary or to Natasha, of whom he seemed even fonder than of his aunt, and clung to them quietly and shyly.

278.44.oldText: When Princess Mary had left Prince Andrew she fully understood what Natasha's face had told her. She did not speak any more to Natasha about hopes of saving his life. She took turns with her beside his sofa, and did not cry anymore, but prayed continually, turning in her soul to that Eternal and Unfathomable, whose presence above the dying man was now so clearly felt.

286.9.oldText: 'It's not too late yet, Your Highness—the enemy hasn't pulled back. If you would order an attack... Otherwise the Guards won't even get a glimpse of smoke.'

305.30.oldText: 'Ah, it's you!' said Petya. 'Are you hungry? Don't be afraid—no one will hurt you. Come in, come in.'

333.28.oldText: At that moment of emotional tenderness, young Nicholas's face—so like his father's—moved Pierre so deeply that after kissing the boy, he quickly stood up, pulled out his handkerchief, and walked to the window.

334.21.oldText: Princess Mary looked from Pierre to Natasha with a gentle smile. In the whole story she saw only Pierre and his goodness. Natasha, leaning on her elbow, her expression constantly changing with the story, watched Pierre without taking her eyes off him for a single moment, clearly living through everything he described along with him.

334.32.oldText: Pierre finished his story. Natasha continued to look at him intently with bright, attentive, animated eyes, as if trying to understand something more that he had perhaps left untold. Pierre, in shy, happy confusion, kept glancing at her and trying to think of something to say that might shift the conversation to a different subject. He began speaking, and Princess Mary too looked at Natasha. She had often been near a woman in love and had seen that look before; she recognized it now on Natasha's face, and she understood.

335.5.oldText: "What—Petersburg? What is Petersburg? Who's in Petersburg?" he asked, though only of himself. "Oh yes, a long time ago—before all this happened—I did mean to go to Petersburg for some reason," he reflected. "Why? But maybe I will go... What a good, considerate fellow he is!" he thought, looking at Savelich. "And what a nice smile!"

336.1.oldText: He did not repeat to himself with a sickening feeling of shame the words he had spoken, or think: "Oh, why didn't I say that?" and "Whatever made me say 'I love you'?" On the contrary, he now replayed in his mind every word he or Natasha had said, down to the smallest detail of her face and smile, and wanted to add nothing and take nothing away. He only wished he could say it all again. "Was it right when she said, 'Leave it to me'? Did she really see into my soul? Yes, she did," Pierre told himself. "And she's wonderful! 'Something fine!'—how she said it! And her eyes. And how she blushed when she said: 'I'll very much look forward to your return'... She loves me. Yes, she loves me." That was the only worry that often troubled Pierre. He made no plans now. The happiness before him seemed so inconceivable that if only he could reach it, there would be nothing beyond. Everything ended there.

336.4.oldText: When people suggested he enter the civil service, or when the war or general political affairs were discussed on the assumption that everyone's well-being depended on some particular turn of events, he would listen with his mild, compassionate smile, and startle everyone with his strange comments. But those who thought they understood Pierre, as well as those who didn't, all felt at this time that he was a delightful and extraordinary person—generous, gentle, clever, cheerful, and magnanimous.

338.12.oldText: It lies in the fact that a historical figure like Alexander I, standing at the highest possible pinnacle of human power, in the blinding light of history focused upon him—exposed to the strongest influences imaginable: the intrigues, flattery, and self-deception inseparable from power, and feeling a responsibility for everything happening in Europe at every moment of his life—proved to be, not fifty years ago but today, not a person of particularly virtuous character. That is what the historians' criticisms amount to.

338.13.oldText: But even if we assume that Alexander was mistaken fifty years ago in his idea of what was good for the people, we must also assume that the historian who judges him will, after some time, also turn out to be wrong in his understanding of what is good for humanity. This assumption is all the more natural and inevitable because the development of history shows us that every year, with every new writer, what we consider good for humanity changes. What once seemed good—giving Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance—is later regarded as harmful. What seems harmful—the Napoleonic wars, the spread of revolutionary ideas—is later recognized as good.

339.9.oldText: We need only acknowledge that we do not know the purpose of the European upheavals, and that we only know the facts—that is, the killings, first in France, then in Italy, Africa, Prussia, Austria, Spain, and Russia—and that the movements from west to east and from east to west form the essential substance of those events. Only then will we no longer need to see something exceptional—some stroke of genius—in the characters of Napoleon and Alexander, and will no longer need to attribute the event to some individual's specific quality.

340.0.oldText: The fundamental significance of the European events at the start of the nineteenth century lies in the mass movement of European peoples from west to east and then from east to west. The initial impulse for the westward movement came from France. For the French to unite into a military force capable of invading the East, they first needed to combine into a sufficiently large group, renounce their established customs and traditions, and—through the process of war and campaigning—develop a leader who could stand at the head of the coming military movement.

340.3.oldText: His colleagues' incompetence, his opponents' weakness and insignificance, the brazenness of his lies, and his dazzling, self-confident narrow-mindedness raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant quality of the soldiers in the Italian campaign, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his own childish boldness and self-assurance win him military glory. Countless so-called coincidences accompany him everywhere. The disfavor into which he falls with the rulers of France works in his favor. His attempts to change his career path fail: he isn't accepted into the Russian army, and his appointment to Turkey comes to nothing.

340.10.oldText: Chance—millions of chances—give him power, and all people, as if by common agreement, work to confirm that power. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him; chance shapes the character of Russia's Paul I, who recognizes his authority; chance produces a plot against him that not only fails to harm him but strengthens his power. Chance throws the Duke of Enghien into his hands and accidentally compels him to kill him, thereby convincing the crowd more effectively than any other means that he has the right to rule, since he possesses the power and the will to use it. Chance arranges it so that though he strains every nerve to prepare an expedition against England—which would certainly have destroyed him—he never carries out that plan, and instead falls upon Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a battle. Chance and genius give him victory after victory. Everything serves him. He is invincible.

340.11.oldText: Like probing movements before a battle, the western forces push eastward several times—in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809—gathering strength and growing. In 1811, the group of people formed in France fuses into one enormous mass with the peoples of central Europe. As this group grows, the man who stands at its head gains more and more justification for his power. During those ten years of preparation, this man forms connections with all the crowned heads of Europe. The rulers of the world, stripped naked by this man, try to oppose him with the ideals of reason and justice. But these seem weak and ridiculous before his ideal of glory and greatness, which makes no sense yet still exerts its force. In their efforts to show him that his plans are wrong, these rulers eagerly humiliate themselves before him. The King of Prussia sends his wife to seek the great man's mercy; the Emperor of Austria considers it a favor that this man accepts the daughter of the Kaisers into his bed. The Pope, guardian of all that the nations hold sacred, uses religion to promote the great man's power. It is not so much Napoleon who prepares himself for the fulfillment of his role as everyone around him who prepares him for the immense responsibility he is about to bear. There is no act, no crime or petty deception, that he commits which is not immediately reflected in the mouths of those around him as a great deed.

344.3.oldText: Having started farming out of necessity, Nicholas soon grew so devoted to it that it became his favorite—and nearly his only—occupation. He was a plain, practical farmer. He didn't like innovations, especially the English methods that were then coming into vogue. He laughed at theoretical treatises on agriculture, had no interest in factories or expensive crops, and didn't obsess over any one part of his operation to the exclusion of the rest. What he always kept in mind was the estate as a whole, not any particular component. What mattered to him was not nitrogen in the soil or oxygen in the air, not special plows or fertilizers, but the principal instrument through which nitrogen, oxygen, plows, and fertilizers all worked—that is, the laboring peasant. When Nicholas first took up farming and began to understand its various branches, it was the peasant who especially engaged his attention. He saw the peasant not merely as a tool but as an end in himself and as a judge. At first he studied the peasant closely, trying to understand what he needed and what he considered good and bad, and only pretended to give orders while in fact learning from the peasants, their methods, and their language. Only when he understood the peasants' tastes and aspirations, had learned to speak their language and grasp the hidden meaning behind their words, and felt himself one of them, did he begin to manage them boldly—that is, to fulfill toward them the duty expected of him.

344.10.oldText: Countess Mary was jealous of this passion of her husband's and regretted that she couldn't share it. But she couldn't grasp the joys and frustrations he drew from that world, so alien and remote to her. She couldn't understand why he was so particularly excited and happy when, having gotten up at dawn and spent the whole morning in the fields or on the threshing floor, he came back to tea from the sowing, mowing, or harvesting. She couldn't understand what made him so delighted when he talked enthusiastically about the prosperous, hardworking peasant Matvei Ermilov who had been up all night with his family carting sheaves, or about having gotten all his grain in before anyone else.

345.8.oldText: Nicholas said nothing. He turned crimson, left her side, and paced up and down the room. He understood what she was crying about, but couldn't immediately agree in his heart that what he had done since childhood—what he considered perfectly normal—was wrong.

347.19.oldText: It happened quite often that in a moment of irritation, husband and wife would argue; but long afterward Pierre would discover—to his surprise and delight—that in his wife's ideas and actions he found the very thought she had argued against, stripped of everything extraneous that his own masculine expression of it had introduced. And he found it there in its purest form.

349.4.oldText: Young Nicholas—now a slim boy of fifteen, delicate and intelligent, with curly light-brown hair and beautiful eyes—was delighted because Uncle Pierre, as he called him, was the object of his rapturous and passionate devotion. No one had deliberately tried to inspire this devotion in him; he had come to it on his own. In his imagination, Pierre was a hero. From half-remembered stories about Pierre and Natasha, from the emotion with which Pierre spoke of the boy's dead father, from the careful, reverent tenderness with which Natasha spoke of him, the boy—who was only just beginning to guess what love is—formed the idea that his father had loved Natasha and had, when dying, bequeathed her to his friend. And that father—whom the boy did not remember—seemed to him a divinity who could not be imagined in human form, and of whom he never thought without a swelling heart and tears of sorrow and enthusiasm. So the boy was happy that Pierre had come.

349.10.oldText: Though he was the most absent-minded and forgetful of men, Pierre had managed—with the help of a list his wife had drawn up—to buy everything, not forgetting his mother-in-law's and brother-in-law's commissions, nor the dress material as a gift for Belova, nor toys for his nephews. In the early days of his marriage, this demand that he remember everything had struck him as strange, and he'd been impressed by the serious way Natasha insisted that he not forget a single item she'd entrusted to him, and by how offended she was when he returned from his first trip having forgotten everything. But in time he grew accustomed to it. Knowing that Natasha never asked him to buy anything for herself, and only gave him commissions for others when he offered, he now took an unexpected, childlike pleasure in buying presents for the whole household—never forgetting anything. If he deserved a scolding from Natasha, it was only for buying too many things and things that were too expensive.

350.0.oldText: When Pierre and his wife entered the drawing room, the countess was in one of her usual states in which she needed the mental effort of playing patience. So—though out of habit she greeted him with the words she always used when Pierre or her son returned: "High time, my dear! We've been waiting and waiting. Thank heaven you're here!"—and when she received her presents said the same words she always said: "It's not the gift that counts, my dear... thank you for thinking of an old woman like me..."—it was clear that Pierre's arrival annoyed her at that moment because it distracted her from her unfinished game. She finished the game and only then examined the presents. They consisted of a card box of splendid workmanship, a bright-blue Sevres teacup with shepherdesses painted on it and a lid, and a gold snuffbox with the late count's portrait on it, which Pierre had commissioned from a miniaturist in Petersburg. The countess had been wanting this for a long time, but now she didn't feel like crying and so she looked at the portrait indifferently and focused instead on the card box.

350.1.oldText: "Thank you, my dear, you've cheered me up," she said, as she always did. "But best of all you've brought yourself back—this has been absolutely ridiculous. You really must scold your wife! What are we to do with her? Without you she's like a madwoman! She doesn't see anything, doesn't remember anything," she said with her usual phrases. "Look, Anna Timofeevna," she added to her companion, "see what a fine card box my son has brought me!"

350.2.oldText: Belova admired the presents and was delighted with her dress material.

350.3.oldText: Though Pierre, Natasha, Nicholas, Countess Mary, and Denisov had much to talk about that they couldn't discuss in front of the old countess—not that anything was hidden from her, but because she had fallen so far behind that if they had started talking about anything in front of her, they would have had to answer her irrelevant questions and repeat things she'd already been told. They would have had to explain that so-and-so was dead, or so-and-so was married, which she would forget again the next time—yet they sat at tea around the samovar in the drawing room, and Pierre answered the old countess's questions that were of no interest to anyone, telling her that Prince Vasili had aged, and that Countess Maria Alexeyevna sent her regards and remembered her kindly, and so on.

350.4.oldText: This kind of conversation, interesting to no one yet unavoidable, continued through teatime. All the grown-up members of the family were assembled around the round tea table where Sonya presided by the samovar. The children with their tutors and governesses had already had tea and could be heard in the next room. Everyone sat in their usual places at tea; Nicholas sat by the stove at a small table where his tea was passed to him; Milka, an old gray borzoi bitch, the daughter of the original Milka, with a face full of black spots, lay in an armchair beside him. Denisov, his curly hair now half-gray, his mustache and whiskers showing it too, sat next to Countess Mary with his general's unbuttoned tunic. Pierre sat between his wife and the old countess. He was telling them what he knew might interest the old lady and what she could understand. He talked about external social events and about those people who had once formed the circle of the old countess's contemporaries—who had once been a real, living, distinct group but who were now for the most part scattered over the world, finishing their earthly course like she was. But to the countess these contemporaries seemed to be the only serious and real society. Natasha could tell by Pierre's animation that his trip had been interesting and that he had much to say that he couldn't talk about in front of the old countess.

350.5.oldText: Denisov, not being a member of the family, didn't understand Pierre's caution and—being besides very interested in what was going on in Petersburg—kept urging Pierre to tell them about what had happened with the Semyonovsky regiment, or about Arakcheyev, or about the Bible Society. Pierre would occasionally get carried away and start talking, but Nicholas and Natasha always steered him back to the health of Prince Ivan Ivanovich and Countess Maria Antonovna.

350.6.oldText: "Well, and all this nonsense—Gossner and Tatarinova?" Denisov asked. "Is that really still going on?"

351.10.oldText: Nicholas, who didn't share Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was very serious and weighty business, and the fact that A had been appointed Minister of This and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such-and-such and the minister something else, all seemed very important to him. And he thought it was his duty to take an interest in it and to question Pierre accordingly.

352.25.oldText: "Well, I don't think you need to blame yourself on his account. Everything the most devoted mother could do for a son, you've done and are doing for him. And of course I'm glad of it. He's a fine boy, a fine boy! This evening he listened to Pierre in a kind of trance. And do you know—when we stood up to go to supper, I looked over and he'd smashed everything on my desk to bits, and he told me about it himself right away. I've never known him to lie. A fine boy, really!" Nicholas repeated, pleased with his assessment.

352.27.oldText: "Well, it won't be long now. Next summer I'll take him to Petersburg," said Nicholas. "Yes, Pierre always was a dreamer and always will be," he continued, returning to the argument that had clearly upset him. "Well, what business is it of mine what goes on there—Arakcheyev's misconduct, and all the rest? What business was it of mine when we got married and I had so many debts that they were threatening to put me in prison? And what about your mother? She could never understand. And now—in a year or two I could show them Otradnoe! And if everything continues as it is, in another three years I'll have paid off all the debts, and then..."

352.31.oldText: Countess Mary listened to her husband and understood everything he told her. She knew that when he thought aloud like this he would sometimes ask what he'd been saying, and be annoyed if he noticed she'd been thinking about something else. But she had to make a considerable effort to pay attention, because what he said didn't interest her at all. She looked at him and—rather than thinking—felt something else entirely. She felt a submissive, tender love for this man who would never understand everything she understood, and she seemed to love him all the more for that, with a touch of passionate tenderness. Besides this feeling, which absorbed her entirely, she was also thinking about her children: she wasn't thinking about them, exactly, but feeling their existence—the need to watch over their health, to feed, to educate. She mentally counted them over, made sure she hadn't forgotten any, and felt at peace.

353.3.oldText: Natasha told Pierre about her brother's life, about how she had suffered and felt dead inside during Pierre's absence, and how she was fonder than ever of Mary, and how Mary was better than her in every way. In saying this, Natasha was genuinely convinced that Mary was better, but she also expected Pierre to disagree with her—and he did.

354.9.oldText: In the first place, the historian describes the activity of individuals who in his opinion directed humanity. One historian considers only monarchs, generals, and ministers as such people, while another includes orators, scholars, reformers, philosophers, and poets as well. But all historians agree that these individuals expressed the will of their time, and that their activity was the direction in which the historical movement flowed.

355.1.oldText: Biographical historians and historians of individual nations understand this force as a power inherent in heroes and rulers. In their accounts, events happen solely through the will of a Napoleon, an Alexander, or whatever person they happen to be describing. The answers these historians give to the question of what force drives events are satisfying only as long as there is just one historian for each event. But as soon as historians of different nations and perspectives begin describing the same event, the answers they give immediately lose all meaning, because this force is understood by each historian not only differently but often in completely opposite ways.

355.3.oldText: According to this view, the power of historical figures—represented as the product of many forces—can no longer be treated as a force that itself produces events. Yet in most cases, universal historians still use the concept of power as a force that independently produces events, treating it as both cause and effect at the same time.

355.6.oldText: A specialist historian describing the campaign of 1813 or the restoration of the Bourbons plainly asserts that these events were produced by the will of Alexander. But the universal historian Gervinus, refuting this view, tries to prove that the campaign of 1813 and the restoration of the Bourbons were caused not only by Alexander but also by Stein, Metternich, Madame de Stael, Talleyrand, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others. The historian has evidently broken down Alexander's power into its components: Talleyrand, Chateaubriand, and the rest. But the sum of these components—that is, the interaction of Chateaubriand, Talleyrand, Madame de Stael, and the others—obviously does not equal the whole result. The fact that millions of Christian men killed one another and devastated Europe was clearly not caused only by these individuals' activity. And therefore, the universal historian—after having broken down Alexander's power into components and proved them insufficient—must again accept the unexplained force called "power" and recognize it as the influence of great men on events, which is precisely the same thing the specialist historian said.

355.9.oldText: The cultural historians are perfectly consistent with their predecessors, the universal historians. If historical events can be explained by the fact that certain people treated one another in certain ways, why not explain them by the fact that certain people wrote certain books? Out of the vast number of indicators that accompany every living phenomenon, these historians select the indicator of intellectual activity and declare it to be the cause. But despite all their efforts to prove that the cause of events lies in intellectual activity, only with great reluctance can one agree that there is any connection between intellectual activity and the movement of peoples—and it is quite impossible to admit that intellectual activity guides the actions of people, because phenomena like the brutal murders of the French Revolution, which resulted from preaching about human equality, do not support such a conclusion.

355.10.oldText: But even granting all the cleverly constructed arguments with which these histories are filled—granting that nations are governed by some undefined force called an "idea"—history's essential question still remains unanswered. To the former power of monarchs and the influence of advisors and other individuals, a new force has now been added: the power of ideas. But how this new force is connected to events—that is, how one particular idea out of the millions of ideas that exist gives rise to a particular event—still needs to be explained.

355.11.oldText: Undoubtedly some relationship exists between all people who live at the same time, and so it is possible to find connections between the intellectual activity of people and their historical movements, just as connections can be found between the movements of humanity and trade, handicrafts, gardening, or anything else you care to name.

357.16.oldText: Some historians—those biographical and specialist historians already mentioned—who in their simplicity fail to grasp the question of what power means, seem to assume that the collective will of the people is unconditionally transferred to historical figures, and therefore when describing any power they treat it as the one real, absolute, and inviolable power.

357.19.oldText: Each historian, according to his own idea of what constitutes a nation's progress, looks for the key conditions in the greatness, wealth, freedom, or enlightenment of the citizens of France or some other country. But not only do historians contradict each other about the nature of this program—even admitting that one such program exists for all nations—the facts of history almost always contradict the theory. If the conditions on which power is delegated are a nation's wealth, freedom, or enlightenment, why did a Louis XIV or an Ivan the Terrible live out their reigns in peace, while a Louis XVI or a Charles I were executed by their peoples? To this question the historians have no answer. If the connection between rulers and peoples is based on conditions, then why should people who violate those conditions be punished—punished by execution or by disgrace—by the very people who put them in power on those conditions?

357.28.oldText: Is the movement of the peoples during the Crusades explained by the lives and activity of the Godfreys and the Louises and their ladies? For us, that movement of peoples from west to east—without leaders, with a crowd of vagabonds and Peter the Hermit—remains incomprehensible. And still more incomprehensible is the cessation of that movement just when a rational and sacred goal for the Crusades—the liberation of Jerusalem—had been clearly set by the historic leaders. Popes, kings, and knights encouraged people to free the Holy Land; but the people did not go, because the unknown cause that had previously driven them to move no longer existed.

358.6.oldText: "If the animals at the front of the herd change, this happens because the collective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to another, depending on whether the animal is or isn't leading them in the direction chosen by the whole herd." This is the answer given by historians who assume the collective will of the masses is transferred to rulers on certain conditions which they regard as known.

358.14.oldText: On one hand, reflection shows that the expression of a person's will—his words—are only part of the total activity expressed in an event, such as a war or a revolution. And so, without invoking some incomprehensible, supernatural force—a miracle—one cannot accept that words can be the immediate cause of the movement of millions of people.

358.15.oldText: On the other hand, even if we admitted that words can be the cause of events, history shows that the expression of historical figures' wills in most cases produces no effect at all—that is, their orders are often not carried out, and sometimes the very opposite of what they commanded takes place.

358.16.oldText: Without admitting divine intervention in human affairs, we cannot regard "power" as the cause of events.

358.17.oldText: Power, from the standpoint of experience, is merely the relationship that exists between the expression of someone's will and the carrying out of that will by others.

358.18.oldText: To explain the conditions of that relationship, we must first establish a concept of the expression of will, referring it to man and not to God.

359.5.oldText: For an order to be reliably carried out, a person must command what can actually be done. But knowing what can and what cannot be done is impossible—not only in the case of Napoleon's invasion of Russia, where millions of people participated, but even in the simplest event—because in either case millions of obstacles may arise.

359.6.oldText: Our mistaken belief that an event is caused by the command that precedes it comes from the fact that, after the event has taken place, out of thousands of commands only those few that happened to match the event are remembered as having been carried out. We forget about the others because they didn't match the event and therefore weren't executed.

360.13.oldText: Examining only those expressions of will by historical persons which, as commands, were connected with events, historians have assumed that the events depended on those commands. But examining the events themselves and the connection in which the historical persons stood to the people, we have found that historical persons and their commands are dependent on events.

361.17.oldText: No matter how often experiment and reasoning show a man that under the same conditions, with the same character, he will do the same thing as before—yet when he approaches for the thousandth time an action that always ends the same way, he feels just as sure as ever that he can act however he wishes. Every man, savage or sage, however irrefutably reason and experience prove to him that it is impossible to imagine two different actions under precisely identical conditions, feels that without this absurd notion—which constitutes the essence of freedom—he cannot imagine life.

361.27.oldText: They say and write and print that the soul and freedom do not exist, that the life of man is expressed by muscular movements, and muscular movements are determined by nervous activity; that the soul and free will do not exist because at some unknown period of time we descended from apes. They say and write and print this not because they suspect that this is what the natural scientists' arguments actually lead to (for you can't cut off a thought in the middle), but because otherwise—if man has no freedom—it would be impossible to live. And man needs to live and to act.

362.10.oldText: A drowning man who grabs another and drags him under; a hungry mother exhausted from nursing who steals food; a soldier trained in discipline who kills a defenseless man on orders—these all seem less guilty, less free, and more subject to the law of necessity, to anyone who knows the circumstances of their actions. And conversely, a man who commits murder out of jealousy with no apparent provocation seems more free and less subject to the law of necessity. In every case, our idea of freedom and necessity depends on the circumstances under which the action took place.

362.25.oldText: When we do not at all understand the cause of an action—whether it is a crime, a good deed, or something morally neutral—we attribute the greatest amount of freedom to it. In the case of a crime, we most urgently demand punishment; in the case of a virtuous act, we rate its merit most highly; in the morally neutral case, we see the most individuality, originality, and independence. But if even one of the countless causes is known to us, we concede a certain amount of necessity and are less insistent in our demand for punishment, less appreciative of the virtue, and less ready to attribute freedom to the seemingly original action.

363.4.oldText: (2) However closely we bring the time of judgment to the time of the deed, we never get a notion of freedom in time. For if I examine an action committed a second ago, I must still recognize it as not free, because it is irrevocably linked to the moment at which it was committed. Can I raise my arm? I raise it; but I ask myself: could I have not raised it at the moment that has already passed? To convince myself that I could have, I don't raise my arm the next moment. But the moment I was asking about was not now—it is already irrecoverably past, and the arm I then raised was in the very air through which I have now refrained from raising it. The moment in which I chose not to raise my arm is a different moment from the moment I did raise it, and the flow of time in which I chose not to act was not the same as the past flow of time in which I acted. Even if I imagine an action in the very earliest moment of the present, unevoked by any cause, the infinitesimal instant of the present as it becomes the past would still contain a minimum of necessity.

365.11.oldText: Just as in astronomy the difficulty of recognizing the motion of the earth lay in abandoning the immediate sensation of the earth's stability and the planets' apparent motion, so in history the difficulty of recognizing the subjection of the individual to the laws of space, time, and cause lies in abandoning the immediate feeling of the independence of one's own personality.

1.0.oldText: [På fransk] »Nå, fyrste, så Genova og Lucca er nu ikke andet end godser, der tilhører familien Bonaparte. Men jeg advarer Dem — hvis De ikke fortæller mig, at dette betyder krig, hvis De fortsætter med at forsvare de grusomheder, den Antikrist begår — og jeg er virkelig overbevist om, at han er Antikrist — så er jeg færdig med Dem. De er ikke længere min ven, ikke længere min 'trofaste slave', som De så gerne kalder Dem selv! Men hvordan har De det? Jeg kan se, at jeg har forskrækket Dem — sæt Dem ned og fortæl mig alle nyhederne.«

1.1.oldText: Det var juli 1805, og den talende var den velkendte Anna Pavlovna Scherer, hofdame og yndling hos kejserinde Marja Fjodorovna. Det var med disse ord, hun modtog fyrst Vasilij Kuragin, en mand af høj rang og indflydelse, som var den første gæst ved hendes selskab. Anna Pavlovna havde hostet i flere dage. Hun led af la grippe, som hun selv sagde — grippe var et nyt modeord i Sankt Petersborg på den tid, og kun eliten brugte det.

9.34.oldText: Englænderen nikkede, men gav intet tegn på, om han selv agtede at tage udfordringen op. Anatole ville ikke slippe ham, og selvom englænderen blev ved med at nikke for at vise, at han forstod, fortsatte Anatole med at oversætte Dolokovs ord til engelsk. En tynd ung fyr — en husar fra livgarden, der havde tabt hele aftenen — klatrede op på vindueskarmen, lænede sig ud og kiggede ned.

9.37.oldText: Dolokhov stillede flasken på vindueskarmen inden for rækkevidde, klatrede langsomt og forsigtigt ud af vinduet og lod benene hænge ned. Han støttede sig mod begge sider af karmen, satte sig til rette, gled en smule til højre, så til venstre, og tog flasken. Anatole bragte to stearinlys og stillede dem på karmen, selvom det allerede var ret lyst. Dolokovs ryg i den hvide skjorte og hans krøllede hoved var oplyst fra begge sider. Alle stimlede sammen ved vinduet — englænderen forrest. Pierre stod og smilede uden at sige noget. En mand, ældre end de øvrige, trængte sig pludselig frem med et udtryk af alarm og vrede og forsøgte at gribe fat i Dolokovs skjorte.

9.43.oldText: Med det vendte han sig om igen, slap med hænderne, tog flasken og førte den til sine læber. Han kastede hovedet bagover og løftede den frie hånd for at holde balancen. En af lakajerne, der havde bøjet sig ned for at samle glasskår op, frøs i den position med blikket låst på vinduet og Dolokovs ryg. Anatole stod stiv med store øjne. Englænderen iagttog fra siden med sammenpressede læber. Manden, der havde forsøgt at stoppe det hele, løb hen i et hjørne og kastede sig ned i sofaen med ansigtet nedad. Pierre dækkede ansigtet med hænderne — et svagt smil hang stadig i hans træk, selvom hans udtryk nu kun viste rædsel og frygt. Alle var fuldstændig stille. Pierre tog hænderne fra øjnene. Dolokhov sad stadig i den samme stilling, kun var hans hoved kastet endnu længere bagover, indtil det krøllede hår berørte hans skjortekrave, og hånden med flasken hævede sig højere og højere, rystende af anstrengelse. Flasken tømtes synligt, hævede sig endnu højere, hovedet tippede endnu mere bagover. »Hvorfor tager det så lang tid?« tænkte Pierre. Det føltes, som om der var gået mere end en halv time. Pludselig buede Dolokovs ryg bagud, og hans arm rystede krampagtigt; dette var nok til at få hele hans krop til at glide på den skrå karme. Da han begyndte at skride, vaklede hans hoved og arm endnu mere under anstrengelsen. Den ene hånd bevægede sig, som for at gribe vindueskarmen, men trak sig så tilbage uden at røre den. Pierre dækkede atter øjnene og lovede sig selv, at han aldrig ville åbne dem igen. Så mærkede han pludselig et røre rundt omkring sig. Han kiggede op: Dolokhov stod på vindueskarmen, bleg men strålende i ansigtet.

9.46.oldText: »Bravo! Godt gjort! Dét var et væddemål! Utroligt!« lød det fra alle sider.

10.3.oldText: [På fransk] »Jeg er Dem så taknemmelig, kære« — han kaldte absolut alle for »kære«, hvad enten de stod over eller under ham i rang, uden den mindste ændring i tone — »jeg takker Dem på mine egne vegne og på vegne af vores to kære, hvis navnedag vi fejrer. Men De må komme til middag — jeg bliver stødt, hvis De ikke gør, kære! På hele familiens vegne insisterer jeg — kom venligst, kære!« Han gentog disse ord til hver eneste gæst uden undtagelse eller variation med det samme udtryk i sit fyldige, muntre, glattbarberede ansigt, det samme faste håndtryk og de samme hurtige, gentagne buk. Så snart han havde fulgt én gæst ud, vendte han tilbage til dem, der stadig var i salonen, trak en stol hen og satte sig med benene bekvemt spredt og hænderne på knæene — stillingen hos en mand, der nyder livet og forstår at leve det — og vippede frem og tilbage med let værdighed, førte småsnak om vejret eller spurgte til nogens helbred, idet han skiftede mellem russisk og meget dårligt men grundigt selvsikkert fransk. Derpå rejste han sig som en mand, der er træt men hengiven til sine pligter, for at følge den næste gæst ud, glattede sit sparsomme grå hår hen over sin isse og inviterede også dem til middag. Undertiden passerede han på vejen tilbage fra forhallen gennem vinterhaven og anretterrummet ind i den store marmorspisestue, hvor der var dækket op til firs gæster. Han iagttog lakajerne, der bar sølvtøj og porcelæn ind, stillede borde op og foldede damaskduger ud, og tilkaldte Dmitrij Vasiljevitj — en mand af god familie, der styrede alle hans anliggender — og sagde med synlig glæde ved synet af det enorme bord: »Nå, Dmitrij, sørg for at alt er i orden! Godt! Det vigtige er serveringen — det er det, der tæller.« Og med et tilfreds suk gik han tilbage til salonen.

10.7.oldText: »Kære grevinde, det er en evighed siden! Hun har været syg, den stakkel — ved Razumovskij-ballet — og grevinde Apraksina — jeg var så henrykt...« Lydene af livlige kvinderstemmer tumlede hen over hinanden og blandede sig med kjolernes raslen og stolenes skraben. Og så begyndte en af de samtaler, der varer netop længe nok til, at gæsterne ved den første pause rejser sig med en raslen af silke og siger: »Jeg er så henrykt... mammas helbred... og grevinde Apraksina...« før de rasler tilbage til forhallen, tager kapper eller mantler på og kører bort. Samtalen faldt på dagens store emne: sygdommen hos den berømt rige og smukke grev Bezukhov — en fejret skikkelse fra Katarinas tid — og hans uægte søn Pierre, den selvsamme unge mand, der havde opført sig så dårligt ved Anna Pavlovnas selskab.

19.22.oldText: »Jeg har fire sønner i hæren, og alligevel jammer jeg ikke. Det ligger altsammen i Guds hænder. Man kan dø i sin seng, eller Gud kan spare én i et slag,« svarede Marja Dmitrijevnas dybe stemme, der ubesværet bar hele bordets længde.

22.0.oldText: Mens disse samtaler foregik i forværelset og i prinsessens værelse, rullede en vogn med Pierre (der var blevet sendt bud efter) og Anna Mikhajlovna (Borís' moder, som fandt det nødvendigt at ledsage ham) ind i gården til grev Bezukhovs palæ. Da hjulene blidt rullede hen over halmen, der var strøet under vinduerne, opdagede Anna Mikhajlovna, der lige havde trøstet sin rejsefælle med venlige ord, at han sad og sov i sit hjørne og vækkede ham. Pierre vågnede, fulgte Anna Mikhajlovna ud af vognen og begyndte først da at tænke på det møde med sin døende far, der ventede ham. Han bemærkede, at de ikke var kørt til hovedindgangen, men til bagdøren. Mens han steg ud af vogntrinnet, så han to mænd, der lignede handlende, løbe hastigt fra indgangen og gemme sig i husets skygge. Pierre lagde også mærke til adskillige andre mænd af samme slags, der skjulte sig i skyggen på begge sider af huset. Men hverken Anna Mikhajlovna eller lakajen eller kusken, der umuligt kunne undgå at se disse mennesker, tog notits af dem. »Det er nok i orden,« tænkte Pierre og fulgte Anna Mikhajlovna. Hun skyndte sig op ad den smalle, dunkelt oplyste stentrappe og kaldte på Pierre, der haltede bagefter, om at følge med. Selvom han ikke kunne se, hvorfor det var nødvendigt for ham overhovedet at besøge greven, endnu mindre hvorfor han skulle gå ad bagtrappen, så bedømte han ud fra Anna Mikhajlovnas beslutsomme og forjagede mine, at det hele var absolut nødvendigt. Halvvejs oppe ad trappen blev de næsten væltet af nogle mænd, der kom løbende ned med spande, mens deres støvler klaskede mod trinene. Disse mænd trykkede sig ind mod væggen for at lade Pierre og Anna Mikhajlovna passere og viste ikke den mindste overraskelse over at se dem dér.

23.2.oldText: Sophie (Sofja), den rosenkindede, lattertilbøjelige yngste prinsesse med skønhedspletten, iagttog ham. Hun smilede, gemte sit ansigt i lommetørklædet og sad et øjeblik med det skjult; så kiggede hun op og fik øje på Pierre og begyndte igen at le. Hun kunne åbenbart ikke se på ham uden at le, men kunne heller ikke lade være med at kigge på ham; så for at undgå fristelsen smuttede hun stille om bag en af søjlerne. Midt i gudstjenesten standsede præsternes stemmer pludselig, de hviskede til hinanden, og den gamle tjener, der holdt grevens hånd, rejste sig og sagde noget til damerne. Anna Mikhajlovna trådte frem, bøjede sig over den døende og vinkede bag sin ryg til Lorrain. Den franske læge holdt ikke noget vokslys; han lænede sig mod en af søjlerne i en ærbødig holdning, der antydede, at han, en udlænding, trods alle forskelle i tro forstod den fulde betydning af den ceremoni, der blev udført, og endda bifaldt den. Han nærmede sig nu den syge med den lydløse gang, der kendetegner et menneske i sin fulde kraft, løftede med sine fine, hvide fingre hånden fri fra det grønne tæppe, vendte sig lidt til siden, følte pulsen og tænkte et øjeblik efter. Den syge fik noget at drikke, der blev uro omkring ham, derefter indtog alle deres pladser igen, og gudstjenesten fortsatte. Under denne pause bemærkede Pierre, at fyrst Vasilij forlod den stol, han havde lænet sig mod, og — med en mine, der sagde, at han vidste, hvad han foretog sig, og at det var de andres problem, hvis de ikke forstod — ikke gik hen til den døende, men passerede forbi ham, sluttede sig til den ældste prinsesse og gik med hende over til den side af rummet, hvor den høje seng med silkegardiner stod. Både fyrst Vasilij og prinsessen forsvandt ud ad en bagdør, men vendte tilbage til deres pladser én efter én, inden gudstjenesten var forbi. Pierre skænkede ikke denne hændelse mere opmærksomhed end resten af, hvad der foregik, da han én gang for alle havde besluttet, at alt, hvad han så ske omkring sig den aften, på en eller anden måde var nødvendigt.
